Shadows cloaked the four resolute figures before us, their forms shrouded in despair. With a heavy heart, we laid upon them the frayed remnants of fabric we had salvaged, then withdrew to secure the door with a firm grip. This forsaken location had become their final resting place, stripped of the dignity that a proper burial or hallowed ground might have offered. Abandoned by society, they had been reduced to mere echoes of forgotten souls, forever stained by the disdain reserved for the seemingly unworthy. The misguided souls who clung to the fleeting hope of immortality would never understand the profound suffering borne by these departed spirits.

We had scarcely taken four paces when the crunch of gravel pierced the stillness, cutting through the quiet like a knife. My heart raced with apprehension, unease clawing at my insides. We dared not be discovered as we fled from that house. Grasping the king's cloak tightly, we sought refuge around the corner of the cabin.

“We're safe for now,” I murmured, urgency tightening my voice. “But that was far too close. Had the night been any brighter, we might have been exposed.”

“Perhaps it was just a wild animal,” the king speculated, struggling to maintain a facade of composure that was fraying under the pressure of the moment.

“True, but any approaching presence could spell danger. We must remain concealed until we are certain the threat has subsided.”

“Listen! Something is coming.”

His instincts proved astute—the footsteps grew louder, encroaching upon our sanctuary. Surely it was merely a creature of the woods; we must have been overreacting. Just as I contemplated moving, I felt the king's firm grip on my arm, urging silence. A tentative knock reverberated against the cabin door, sending chills racing down my spine. A second knock quickly followed, accompanied by a frantic voice calling out:

“Mother! Father! Open the door—we've escaped and come bearing news that will chill your hearts yet lift your spirits! We cannot linger here; we must flee! But where are you? Mother! Father!”

With urgency coursing through me, I pulled the king toward the hut's rear corner. “We must act—now.”

The king hesitated, ready to voice his doubts, but then the door creaked open, revealing mourners steeped in grief amid the scattered remnants of their loved ones.

“Come, my liege! A fire will soon be lit, and what follows will break your heart.”

With those words, he sprang into action without hesitation. As we emerged onto the path, I quickened my pace, and soon he shed his regal demeanor to match my speed. I fought to suppress the sorrow over the scene we had left behind, redirecting our conversation.

“I have faced the affliction that claimed those lives; fear no longer binds me. But if you—”

He interrupted, concern etched deeply into his brow. “It’s not the illness that troubles me; it’s the escape of the young men. How could they have dared such defiance? Their lord never granted them freedom.”

“I am certain they fled,” I reassured him.

“That notion only heightens my anxiety—your suspicions trouble me.”

“I hesitate to frame it in such stark terms. While I believe in their freedom, I harbor no regret.”

“I think I share your sentiment, yet—”

“What weighs upon your mind?” I inquired, sensing the heaviness of his unease.

“If they truly escaped, it may force us to confront their lord. A man of his standing cannot tolerate such open rebellion from those of their lowly status.”

Once again, his narrow perspective unsettled me. Raised in privilege and cloaked in an instinctive sense of superiority, he perceived only one facet of the situation. To him, imprisoning those men without reason while their families languished in hunger was justifiable; they were peasants, at the mercy of their lord’s whims, however arbitrary. Yet the very notion of those men breaking free from their unjust captivity was a scandal he could not accept.

For what felt like an eternity, I wrestled with guiding our discussion until a flicker of red light captured our attention as we crested a small hill.

“Look, a fire,” I remarked, captivated by its flickering glow.

The sight enchanted me; I had long nurtured dreams of establishing an insurance enterprise, training horses, and developing steam fire engines that would ultimately create a paid fire department. The clergy had condemned my aspirations in fire and life insurance as acts of arrogance against divine will. I argued that my endeavors did not contradict God’s designs but alleviated dire consequences; they insisted my rationale mirrored gambling against divine decrees—equally sinful. Though they thwarted many of my efforts, I continued to thrive in accident insurance. Knights, traditionally rather dim-witted and steeped in superstition, occasionally grasped the logical foundation of my offerings. Thus, during a recent tournament clean-up, it was almost inevitable to stumble upon a handful of my accident tickets tangled among discarded helmets.

For a time, we lingered in the oppressive darkness, entranced by the distant crimson glow, straining to unravel the elusive whispers that ebbed and flowed around us. Occasionally, the sounds crescendoed, seeming to draw nearer, but just as we craned our necks to discern their source, they would dissolve back into the void, carrying their mysteries with them. As we began our descent down the hill, the winding path led us into an almost impenetrable shroud of night, nestled among towering trees. After traversing perhaps half a mile, the murmurs coalesced, but an approaching storm unleashed gusts of wind, flashes of lightning, and distant thunder.

With unwavering resolve, I pressed onward until I collided with something soft and heavy beneath my weight. In that moment, a flash of lightning illuminated a horrific sight—a man's contorted face dangled from a tree branch, swaying in the wind! It seemed to writhe in agony, yet it was merely an grotesque illusion made by the light. A jolt of terror surged through me. Thunder erupted in a deafening roar, and torrential rain began to pour from the heavens. We had to act quickly to cut him down, praying for a glimmer of life within him. The lightning crackled with increasing frequency, casting sharp contrasts of light and shadow around us. One moment, the man hung starkly illuminated; the next, he vanished into the encroaching darkness.

“We must save him,” I implored, my voice charged with urgency.

He countered my plea, “If he took his own life, he willingly surrendered his existence to his lord; let him be. If others hung him, perhaps they had their reasons—why should we intervene?”

“But—”

“No ‘buts’! Leave him be. Moreover, when the lightning strikes again—look over there.”

Two more bodies hung lifelessly, no more than fifty yards away!

“This is no time for futile kindness toward the dead. They no longer require your compassion. Come—it’s pointless to linger here.”

At midnight all was over, and we sat in the presence of four corpses. We covered them with such rags as we could find, and started away, fastening the door behind us. Their home must be these people's grave, for they could not have Christian burial, or be admitted to consecrated ground. They were as dogs, wild beasts, lepers, and no soul that valued its hope of eternal life would throw it away by meddling in any sort with these rebuked and smitten outcasts.

We had not moved four steps when I caught a sound as of footsteps upon gravel. My heart flew to my throat. We must not be seen coming from that house. I plucked at the king's robe and we drew back and took shelter behind the corner of the cabin.

“Now we are safe,” I said, “but it was a close call--so to speak. If the night had been lighter he might have seen us, no doubt, he seemed to be so near.”

“Mayhap it is but a beast and not a man at all.”

“True. But man or beast, it will be wise to stay here a minute and let it get by and out of the way.”

“Hark! It cometh hither.”

True again. The step was coming toward us--straight toward the hut. It must be a beast, then, and we might as well have saved our trepidation. I was going to step out, but the king laid his hand upon my arm. There was a moment of silence, then we heard a soft knock on the cabin door. It made me shiver. Presently the knock was repeated, and then we heard these words in a guarded voice:

“Mother! Father! Open--we have got free, and we bring news to pale your cheeks but glad your hearts; and we may not tarry, but must fly! And--but they answer not. Mother! father!--”

I drew the king toward the other end of the hut and whispered:

“Come--now we can get to the road.”

The king hesitated, was going to demur; but just then we heard the door give way, and knew that those desolate men were in the presence of their dead.

“Come, my liege! in a moment they will strike a light, and then will follow that which it would break your heart to hear.”

He did not hesitate this time. The moment we were in the road I ran; and after a moment he threw dignity aside and followed. I did not want to think of what was happening in the hut--I couldn't bear it; I wanted to drive it out of my mind; so I struck into the first subject that lay under that one in my mind:

“I have had the disease those people died of, and so have nothing to fear; but if you have not had it also--”

He broke in upon me to say he was in trouble, and it was his conscience that was troubling him:

“These young men have got free, they say--but _how_? It is not likely that their lord hath set them free.”

“Oh, no, I make no doubt they escaped.”

“That is my trouble; I have a fear that this is so, and your suspicion doth confirm it, you having the same fear.”

“I should not call it by that name though. I do suspect that they escaped, but if they did, I am not sorry, certainly.”

“I am not sorry, I _think_--but--”

“What is it? What is there for one to be troubled about?”

“_If_ they did escape, then are we bound in duty to lay hands upon them and deliver them again to their lord; for it is not seemly that one of his quality should suffer a so insolent and high-handed outrage from persons of their base degree.”

There it was again. He could see only one side of it. He was born so, educated so, his veins were full of ancestral blood that was rotten with this sort of unconscious brutality, brought down by inheritance from a long procession of hearts that had each done its share toward poisoning the stream. To imprison these men without proof, and starve their kindred, was no harm, for they were merely peasants and subject to the will and pleasure of their lord, no matter what fearful form it might take; but for these men to break out of unjust captivity was insult and outrage, and a thing not to be countenanced by any conscientious person who knew his duty to his sacred caste.

I worked more than half an hour before I got him to change the subject--and even then an outside matter did it for me. This was a something which caught our eyes as we struck the summit of a small hill--a red glow, a good way off.

“That's a fire,” said I.

Fires interested me considerably, because I was getting a good deal of an insurance business started, and was also training some horses and building some steam fire-engines, with an eye to a paid fire department by and by. The priests opposed both my fire and life insurance, on the ground that it was an insolent attempt to hinder the decrees of God; and if you pointed out that they did not hinder the decrees in the least, but only modified the hard consequences of them if you took out policies and had luck, they retorted that that was gambling against the decrees of God, and was just as bad. So they managed to damage those industries more or less, but I got even on my accident business. As a rule, a knight is a lummux, and sometimes even a labrick, and hence open to pretty poor arguments when they come glibly from a superstition-monger, but even _he_ could see the practical side of a thing once in a while; and so of late you couldn't clean up a tournament and pile the result without finding one of my accident-tickets in every helmet.

We stood there awhile, in the thick darkness and stillness, looking toward the red blur in the distance, and trying to make out the meaning of a far-away murmur that rose and fell fitfully on the night. Sometimes it swelled up and for a moment seemed less remote; but when we were hopefully expecting it to betray its cause and nature, it dulled and sank again, carrying its mystery with it. We started down the hill in its direction, and the winding road plunged us at once into almost solid darkness--darkness that was packed and crammed in between two tall forest walls. We groped along down for half a mile, perhaps, that murmur growing more and more distinct all the time. The coming storm threatening more and more, with now and then a little shiver of wind, a faint show of lightning, and dull grumblings of distant thunder. I was in the lead. I ran against something--a soft heavy something which gave, slightly, to the impulse of my weight; at the same moment the lightning glared out, and within a foot of my face was the writhing face of a man who was hanging from the limb of a tree! That is, it seemed to be writhing, but it was not. It was a grewsome sight. Straightway there was an ear-splitting explosion of thunder, and the bottom of heaven fell out; the rain poured down in a deluge. No matter, we must try to cut this man down, on the chance that there might be life in him yet, mustn't we? The lightning came quick and sharp now, and the place was alternately noonday and midnight. One moment the man would be hanging before me in an intense light, and the next he was blotted out again in the darkness. I told the king we must cut him down. The king at once objected.

“If he hanged himself, he was willing to lose him property to his lord; so let him be. If others hanged him, belike they had the right--let him hang.”

“But--”

“But me no buts, but even leave him as he is. And for yet another reason. When the lightning cometh again--there, look abroad.”

Two others hanging, within fifty yards of us!

“It is not weather meet for doing useless courtesies unto dead folk. They are past thanking you. Come--it is unprofitable to tarry here.”

Walking beside her, he felt irresistibly drawn to her whimsical charm and remarked, “Coketown possesses a unique vitality, doesn’t it?”

“Indeed! But I must caution you against embarking on such journeys too frequently, dear lady,” he said, genuine concern threading through his tone.

“Oh, there’s no need for worry! It’s only once a year!” she chuckled, shaking her head in amusement. “I save my pennies for this beloved event—an annual pilgrimage to wander the streets and watch the gentlemen.”

“Is that truly the extent of your adventures?” Stephen asked, astonishment tinting his voice.

“That in itself brings me immense joy,” she answered earnestly. “I desire nothing more! I’ve been here, waiting for a fleeting glimpse of that gentleman,” she added, gesturing toward Mr. Bounderby as he passed by. “Yet he seems delayed this year. Should I leave without even a whisper of recognition, I shall still find contentment in having met you instead, even if he remains elusive.” With that, she scrutinized Stephen closely, committing his features to memory, though the sparkle in her eyes dimmed slightly.

He marveled at the lengths one would go for a mere glimpse of another. As they neared the church, he noticed the clock and quickened his pace.

“Are you heading to work?” she asked, effortlessly matching his stride.

“Yes, time is of the essence,” he replied. The moment he mentioned his profession, her demeanor noticeably shifted.

“Aren’t you happy?” she asked, concern lacing her voice.

“Well, everyone carries their own burdens, madam,” he replied, careful not to shatter her cheerful image of the life he led—which she most likely envisioned as filled with joy. He was acutely aware of life’s challenges, yet if this wise and weathered woman found solace in believing his struggles were light, he would gladly grant her that small comfort, even if it did little to lift his own heavy heart.

“Ah, I see! Domestic troubles, perhaps?” she suggested, nodding with understanding.

“Occasionally, yes,” he admitted, striving to maintain a composed facade.

“But surely a gentleman like you wouldn’t let such troubles impede your work?” she pressed gently.

“No, no; they remain in the background while I labor,” Stephen assured her. In that realm, all was as it should be. (He refrained from elaborating—out of kindness—on the recent grand claims of divine entitlement that threatened to disturb that fragile peace.)

As they turned onto a dimly lit side street, workers began to filter in. The church bell tolled, machinery roared to life with relentless efficiency, and the day’s toil commenced. The enchanted elderly woman declared that the bell's chime was the sweetest sound she had ever known.

As he paused to bid her farewell before entering the factory, she asked about the duration of his service there.

“I must kiss the hand,” she insisted, “that has labored in this fine factory for those twelve long years!” Ignoring his protests, she took his hand and pressed her lips to it. Hardly had he begun his work at the loom when, as he adjusted it momentarily, he caught sight of her still gazing in awe at the towering structure through the corner window. He was going to his work? the old woman said, quickening hers, too, quite easily. Yes, time was nearly out. On his telling her where he worked, the old woman became a more singular old woman than before.

‘An’t you happy?’ she asked him.

Their conflict was rooted not in personal animosity but rather in a deep-seated political rivalry stemming from an election Kenneth's father had once won against Hugh Townley. This animus was profound, forcing Ursula to arrange secret meetings with her beloved whenever they could.

“Was MacNair a Conservative or a Grit?” Felicity inquired, her curiosity piqued.

“Does it even matter?” snapped the Story Girl, annoyance creeping into her voice. “In those days, even a Tory could be seen as romantic. Kenneth lived fifteen miles away and spent most of his time at sea, which made their encounters exceedingly rare. It had been nearly three months since their last meeting. Just last Sunday, young Sandy MacNair undertook a grueling journey of eight miles barefoot to attend church in Carlyle. After persuading a fisherman to ferry him across the channel, he trekked another eight miles—not out of piety, but to uphold a promise to his cherished brother, Kenneth. Amid the tumult after the service, he discreetly handed Ursula a letter inviting her to meet Kenneth the following afternoon. Thus, unnoticed, Ursula slipped away while her watchful father and stepmother believed her busy spinning in the loft.

“It was terribly inappropriate of her to mislead her parents,” Felicity interjected, her disapproval evident.

Recognizing Felicity’s disapproving gaze, the Story Girl deftly navigated the ethical dilemma. 

“I’m not here to judge Ursula Townley’s choices,” she replied with a hint of condescension. “I am simply recounting events as they transpired. If what you desire is silence, then by all means remain quiet; after all, stories would cease to exist if perfect behavior were the only guiding principle. When Kenneth finally arrived, their reunion unfolded as one might expect of two lovers longing for each other. Ursula broke the silence, her voice a mix of excitement and anxiety:

“‘Kenneth, I can’t stay—I’ll be missed! You mentioned something important in your letter. What is it?’

“‘My dearest Ursula, listen closely: next Saturday morning, my ship, The Fair Lady, will set sail at dawn from Charlottetown harbor, bound for Buenos Ayres. The timing couldn’t be more perfect; it allows for a splendid return by May.’

“‘Oh, Kenneth!’ Ursula gasped, her color draining as tears threatened to spill. ‘How can you possibly leave me? You’re being so cruel!’

“‘Not at all, my love,’ Kenneth chuckled, warmth emanating from him. ‘The captain of The Fair Lady has every intention of taking his bride on board. We will spend our honeymoon at sea, escaping the chill of a Canadian winter beneath the Southern palms.’

“‘Are you suggesting that I should elope with you, Kenneth?’ she faltered, disbelief saturating her tone.

“‘Precisely, my sweet girl—it’s our only choice!’

“‘Oh, I cannot!’ she protested vehemently. ‘What will Father say—’

“‘We need not inform him—not until it’s too late. Come, Ursula, you know this is the only path forward. Your father will never forgive me for my past transgressions. You cannot abandon me; imagine the heartache of parting if I must embark on this journey alone. Be brave, and let the Townleys and MacNairs pretend their old hostilities persist while we sail on The Fair Lady. I have devised a plan.’

“‘I’m all ears,’ Ursula replied, determination igniting within her.

“‘There’s a dance at The Springs this Friday night. Will you be attending, Ursula?’

“‘Yes, of course.’

“‘Excellent. Though I have no invitation, I will conceal myself in the fir grove behind the house with two horses. When the gathering reaches its peak, you’ll slip out to meet me. It’s just a fifteen-mile ride to Charlottetown, where a kind minister—a friend of mine—will be waiting to marry us. By the time the dancers grow weary, we’ll be aboard our ship, laughing in defiance of fate.’

“‘And what if I refuse to meet you in the fir grove?’ Ursula countered, a flicker of defiance lighting her eyes.

“‘If you don’t, I will sail for South America at dawn the very next day, and many years may pass before Kenneth MacNair returns to these shores.’

“Whether Kenneth understood the weight of his words, Ursula felt their enormity, her resolve faltering. Viewed through Felicity's moral lens, her choice seemed undeniably flawed. Ursula should have assertively declared, ‘No, I shall marry with dignity from my home, donning a lovely gown, surrounded by bridesmaids and gifts galore.’ Yet, she uttered none of that. Caution was a quality Ursula notably lacked—one that Felicity King would have surely cherished.

“You mean she was an audacious hussy,” Felicity retorted, projecting her frustrations onto the long-gone Ursula.

“Oh no, dear Felicity, she was merely a young woman ablaze with passion. I daresay I might have acted similarly. As the eve of the dance approached, Ursula steeled herself with fierce determination. She prepared to journey to The Springs alongside her aunt and uncle, who would arrive on horseback that afternoon, continuing in Old Hugh's carriage—the only mode of transportation in Carlyle at that time. Their plan was to leave early enough to reach their destination before nightfall, for October nights cast ominous shadows, and the woodland paths were fraught with danger.

“As she gazed at her reflection in the mirror, pride swelled within Ursula. Yes, Felicity, she was surely self-assured, but such traits endure through the ages. And she had every reason to feel proud; she donned a sea-green silk gown, freshly imported from England and worn only once before—at a Christmas ball at Government House. The delicate rustling of the fabric enhanced the rosy tint of her cheeks, the sparkle in her eyes, and the sheen of her luxurious chestnut hair. Yet, just as she turned from the glass, an outburst of anger erupted below—the unmistakable roar of her father’s fury.

“Feeling her palms grow clammy, she dashed into the hall, only to find her father storming up the stairs, his face contorted in rage. Below, her stepmother appeared anxious and distressed while Malcolm Ramsay—her neighbor and an unwelcome suitor—stood awkwardly in the doorway, brimming with unspoken admiration.

“‘Ursula!’ Old Hugh bellowed, ‘Come here and put an end to this scoundrel’s lies! He claims you met Kenneth MacNair in the beech grove last Tuesday. Tell him he’s mistaken!’

“Unfazed by the confrontation, Ursula shot Ramsay a scathing glare.

“‘He’s nothing but a dull spy and a gossip,’ she declared boldly, ‘and in this case, he speaks the truth. I did indeed meet Kenneth MacNair last Tuesday.’

“‘And you have the audacity to confess this to my face!’ Hugh roared. ‘Back to your room, girl! Strip off that finery. You will attend no more dances! You shall remain in your chamber until I say otherwise. Not a word! I swear I’ll keep you there if you defy me. Go on—knit your projects instead of wasting your feet twirling at The Springs!’

“He flung a tightly wound ball of gray yarn into her room. Realizing she would need to retrieve it to avoid being treated like a disobedient child, Ursula shot Ramsay a steely glare—he flinched under her scrutiny—before striding away with her chin held high. In the very next moment, she heard the door lock behind her.

“Frustration, humiliation, and disappointment surged within her, prompting a torrent of tears. Yet weeping would change nothing; soon she began to pace her confined quarters. The sound of her uncle and aunt’s carriage departing only heightened her distress.

“What am I to do?” she sighed. “Kenneth will be furious. He’ll believe I’ve forsaken him and leave in a fit of rage. If only I could send him a message; I know he wouldn’t abandon me. But how can I escape? They say where there’s a will, there’s a way. Oh, I’m losing my mind! If only the window weren’t so high, I’d leap from it. Breaking my legs or neck wouldn’t solve anything.”

As the afternoon light began to dim, Ursula heard the rhythmic sound of hoofbeats and rushed to the window. Andrew Kinnear of The Springs was tending to his horse outside. A striking young man and a friend of her father’s, he clearly intended to attend the dance that evening. If only she could speak to him, even for a moment! As soon as he stepped inside, impatience sparked within her, leading her to trip over the tangled ball of yarn her father had discarded. Annoyed, she glared at the yarn before a flash of inspiration ignited within her.

In a frenzy, she penned a note to Kenneth MacNair. Once finished, she unraveled a generous length of gray yarn, secured her letter within, and rewound the ball. A gray ball, blending with the encroaching dusk, would attract far less attention than a fluttering letter dropped from above. With utmost care, she cracked open the window and awaited her moment. As twilight enveloped the landscape, Andrew emerged from the house. To her relief, her father remained oblivious.

As Andrew untethered his horse, Ursula took aim, and with uncanny precision, the ball struck him directly on the head. He looked up, craning his neck to seek her out, and leaning out, she silenced him with a finger pressed to her lips, nodding toward the ball. Though bewildered, Andrew retrieved the yarn, mounted his horse, and galloped away. So far, so good, thought Ursula. But would Andrew grasp its significance? Would he be swift enough to unearth the note hidden within that knobbly ball? And would he even attend the dance?

The hours dripped agonizingly for Ursula; time had never before dragged so painfully. Sleep eluded her, and it was not until midnight that the familiar sound of gravel crunching beneath hooves finally reached her ears. Leaning out, joy surged within her as she caught sight of Kenneth MacNair lurking in the shadows below.

“Oh, Kenneth, did you receive my letter? Is it safe for you to be here?” she whispered urgently.

“As safe as can be,” he replied. “Your father is asleep. I waited two hours down the road until his light finally flickered out, staying an additional half-hour to ensure he was truly snoring. The horses are ready. Slip down and join me, Ursula! We must reach Charlottetown before dawn!”

“That sounds simple enough to say, but I’m locked inside,” she murmured in response. “Go to the back of the barn and fetch the ladder you’ll find there.”

In mere minutes, cloaked in shadows, Ursula descended quietly, and soon they were racing down the road together.

“It’s going to be a difficult journey, Ursula,” Kenneth warned, urgency lacing his words.

“I would gallop to the ends of the earth with you, Kenneth MacNair,” she declared resolutely. Perhaps such a spontaneous declaration might seem imprudent, Felicity would argue, but societal conventions were more lenient back in those days. As the gentle glow of an exquisite October dawn unfurled across the gray sea, The Fair Lady lifted her sails from Charlottetown harbor, with Kenneth and Ursula standing proudly on deck, the bride clutching her most treasured possession: the ball of gray homespun yarn.

“Well,” Dan yawned, “that’s the kind of tale I enjoy! At least no one dies!”

“Did Old Hugh ever forgive Ursula?” I asked, curiosity alight.

“The story halts there in the old tome,” the Story Girl replied, “but the Awkward Man insists that, in time, he did.”

“I can only imagine how romantic it must have been to be swept away like that,” Cecily sighed, her eyes shimmering with wistful longing.

“Don’t you dare indulge in such fanciful dreams, Cecily King,” Felicity admonished sternly.

"One day, over a hundred years ago, Ursula Townley was waiting for Kenneth MacNair in a great beechwood, where brown nuts were falling and an October wind was making the leaves dance on the ground like pixy-people."

"What are pixy-people?" demanded Peter, forgetting the Story Girl's dislike of interruptions.

"Hush," whispered Cecily. "That is only one of the Awkward Man's poetical touches, I guess."

"There were cultivated fields between the grove and the dark blue gulf; but far behind and on each side were woods, for Prince Edward Island a hundred years ago was not what it is today. The settlements were few and scattered, and the population so scanty that old Hugh Townley boasted that he knew every man, woman and child in it. Old Hugh was quite a noted man in his day. He was noted for several things--he was rich, he was hospitable, he was proud, he was masterful--and he had for daughter the handsomest young woman in Prince Edward Island. Of course, the young men were not blind to her good looks, and she had so many lovers that all the other girls hated her--"

"You bet!" said Dan, aside--

"--But the only one who found favour in her eyes was the very last man she should have pitched her fancy on, at least if old Hugh were the judge. Kenneth MacNair was a dark-eyed young sea-captain of the next settlement, and it was to meet him that Ursula stole to the beechwood on that autumn day of crisp wind and ripe sunshine. Old Hugh had forbidden his house to the young man, making such a scene of fury about it that even Ursula's high spirit quailed. Old Hugh had really nothing against Kenneth himself; but years before either Kenneth or Ursula was born, Kenneth's father had beaten Hugh Townley in a hotly contested election. Political feeling ran high in those days, and old Hugh had never forgiven the MacNair his victory. The feud between the families dated from that tempest in the provincial teapot, and the surplus of votes on the wrong side was the reason why, thirty years after, Ursula had to meet her lover by stealth if she met him at all."

"Was the MacNair a Conservative or a Grit?" asked Felicity.

"It doesn't make any difference what he was," said the Story Girl impatiently. "Even a Tory would be romantic a hundred years ago. Well, Ursula couldn't see Kenneth very often, for Kenneth lived fifteen miles away and was often absent from home in his vessel. On this particular day it was nearly three months since they had met. The Sunday before, young Sandy MacNair had been in Carlyle church. He had risen at dawn that morning, walked bare-footed for eight miles along the shore, carrying his shoes, hired a harbour fisherman to row him over the channel, and then walked eight miles more to the church at Carlyle, less, it is to be feared, from a zeal for holy things than that he might do an errand for his adored brother, Kenneth. He carried a letter which he contrived to pass into Ursula's hand in the crowd as the people came out. This letter asked Ursula to meet Kenneth in the beechwood the next afternoon, and so she stole away there when suspicious father and watchful stepmother thought she was spinning in the granary loft."

"It was very wrong of her to deceive her parents," said Felicity primly.

The Story Girl couldn't deny this, so she evaded the ethical side of the question skilfully.

"I am not telling you what Ursula Townley ought to have done," she said loftily. "I am only telling you what she DID do. If you don't want to hear it you needn't listen, of course. There wouldn't be many stories to tell if nobody ever did anything she shouldn't do. Well, when Kenneth came, the meeting was just what might have been expected between two lovers who had taken their last kiss three months before. So it was a good half-hour before Ursula said,

"'Oh, Kenneth, I cannot stay long--I shall be missed. You said in your letter that you had something important to talk of. What is it?'

"'My news is this, Ursula. Next Saturday morning my vessel, The Fair Lady, with her captain on board, sails at dawn from Charlottetown harbour, bound for Buenos Ayres. At this season this means a safe and sure return--next May.'

"'Kenneth!' cried Ursula. She turned pale and burst into tears. 'How can you think of leaving me? Oh, you are cruel!'

"'Why, no, sweetheart,' laughed Kenneth. 'The captain of The Fair Lady will take his bride with him. We'll spend our honeymoon on the high seas, Ursula, and the cold Canadian winter under southern palms.'

"'You want me to run away with you, Kenneth?' exclaimed Ursula.

"'Indeed, dear girl, there's nothing else to do!'

"'Oh, I cannot!' she protested. 'My father would--'

"'We'll not consult him--until afterward. Come, Ursula, you know there's no other way. We've always known it must come to this. YOUR father will never forgive me for MY father. You won't fail me now. Think of the long parting if you send me away alone on such a voyage. Pluck up your courage, and we'll let Townleys and MacNairs whistle their mouldy feuds down the wind while we sail southward in The Fair Lady. I have a plan.'

"'Let me hear it,' said Ursula, beginning to get back her breath.

"'There is to be a dance at The Springs Friday night. Are you invited, Ursula?'

"'Yes.'

"'Good. I am not--but I shall be there--in the fir grove behind the house, with two horses. When the dancing is at its height you'll steal out to meet me. Then 'tis but a fifteen mile ride to Charlottetown, where a good minister, who is a friend of mine, will be ready to marry us. By the time the dancers have tired their heels you and I will be on our vessel, able to snap our fingers at fate.'

"'And what if I do not meet you in the fir grove?' said Ursula, a little impertinently.

"'If you do not, I'll sail for South America the next morning, and many a long year will pass ere Kenneth MacNair comes home again.'

"Perhaps Kenneth didn't mean that, but Ursula thought he did, and it decided her. She agreed to run away with him. Yes, of course that was wrong, too, Felicity. She ought to have said, 'No, I shall be married respectably from home, and have a wedding and a silk dress and bridesmaids and lots of presents.' But she didn't. She wasn't as prudent as Felicity King would have been."

"She was a shameless hussy," said Felicity, venting on the long-dead Ursula that anger she dare not visit on the Story Girl.

"Oh, no, Felicity dear, she was just a lass of spirit. I'd have done the same. And when Friday night came she began to dress for the dance with a brave heart. She was to go to The Springs with her uncle and aunt, who were coming on horseback that afternoon, and would then go on to The Springs in old Hugh's carriage, which was the only one in Carlyle then. They were to leave in time to reach The Springs before nightfall, for the October nights were dark and the wooded roads rough for travelling. When Ursula was ready she looked at herself in the glass with a good deal of satisfaction. Yes, Felicity, she was a vain baggage, that same Ursula, but that kind didn't all die out a hundred years ago. And she had good reason for being vain. She wore the sea-green silk which had been brought out from England a year before and worn but once--at the Christmas ball at Government House. A fine, stiff, rustling silk it was, and over it shone Ursula's crimson cheeks and gleaming eyes, and masses of nut brown hair. As she turned from the glass she heard her father's voice below, loud and angry. Growing very pale, she ran out into the hall. Her father was already half way upstairs, his face red with fury. In the hall below Ursula saw her step-mother, looking troubled and vexed. At the door stood Malcolm Ramsay, a homely neighbour youth who had been courting Ursula in his clumsy way ever since she grew up. Ursula had always hated him.

"'Ursula!' shouted old Hugh, 'come here and tell this scoundrel he lies. He says that you met Kenneth MacNair in the beechgrove last Tuesday. Tell him he lies! Tell him he lies!'

"Ursula was no coward. She looked scornfully at poor Ramsay.

"'The creature is a spy and a tale-bearer,' she said, 'but in this he does not lie. I DID meet Kenneth MacNair last Tuesday.'

"'And you dare to tell me this to my face!' roared old Hugh. 'Back to your room, girl! Back to your room and stay there! Take off that finery. You go to no more dances. You shall stay in that room until I choose to let you out. No, not a word! I'll put you there if you don't go. In with you--ay, and take your knitting with you. Occupy yourself with that this evening instead of kicking your heels at The Springs!'

"He snatched a roll of gray stocking from the hall table and flung it into Ursula's room. Ursula knew she would have to follow it, or be picked up and carried in like a naughty child. So she gave the miserable Ramsay a look that made him cringe, and swept into her room with her head in the air. The next moment she heard the door locked behind her. Her first proceeding was to have a cry of anger and shame and disappointment. That did no good, and then she took to marching up and down her room. It did not calm her to hear the rumble of the carriage out of the gate as her uncle and aunt departed.

"'Oh, what's to be done?' she sobbed. 'Kenneth will be furious. He will think I have failed him and he will go away hot with anger against me. If I could only send a word of explanation I know he would not leave me. But there seems to be no way at all--though I have heard that there's always a way when there's a will. Oh, I shall go mad! If the window were not so high I would jump out of it. But to break my legs or my neck would not mend the matter.'

"The afternoon passed on. At sunset Ursula heard hoof-beats and ran to the window. Andrew Kinnear of The Springs was tying his horse at the door. He was a dashing young fellow, and a political crony of old Hugh. No doubt he would be at the dance that night. Oh, if she could get speech for but a moment with him! When he had gone into the house, Ursula, turning impatiently from the window, tripped and almost fell over the big ball of homespun yarn her father had flung on the floor. For a moment she gazed at it resentfully--then, with a gay little laugh, she pounced on it. The next moment she was at her table, writing a brief note to Kenneth MacNair. When it was written, Ursula unwound the gray ball to a considerable depth, pinned the note on it, and rewound the yarn over it. A gray ball, the color of the twilight, might escape observation, where a white missive fluttering down from an upper window would surely be seen by someone. Then she softly opened her window and waited. It was dusk when Andrew went away. Fortunately old Hugh did not come to the door with him. As Andrew untied his horse Ursula threw the ball with such good aim that it struck him, as she had meant it to do, squarely on the head. Andrew looked up at her window. She leaned out, put her finger warningly on her lips, pointed to the ball, and nodded. Andrew, looking somewhat puzzled, picked up the ball, sprang to his saddle, and galloped off. So far, well, thought Ursula. But would Andrew understand? Would he have wit enough to think of exploring the big, knobby ball for its delicate secret? And would he be at the dance after all? The evening dragged by. Time had never seemed so long to Ursula. She could not rest or sleep. It was midnight before she heard the patter of a handful of gravel on her window-panes. In a trice she was leaning out. Below in the darkness stood Kenneth MacNair.

"'Oh, Kenneth, did you get my letter? And is it safe for you to be here?'

"'Safe enough. Your father is in bed. I've waited two hours down the road for his light to go out, and an extra half-hour to put him to sleep. The horses are there. Slip down and out, Ursula. We'll make Charlottetown by dawn yet.'

"'That's easier said than done, lad. I'm locked in. But do you go out behind the new barn and bring the ladder you will find there.'

"Five minutes later, Miss Ursula, hooded and cloaked, scrambled soundlessly down the ladder, and in five more minutes she and Kenneth were riding along the road.

"'There's a stiff gallop before us, Ursula,' said Kenneth.

"'I would ride to the world's end with you, Kenneth MacNair,' said Ursula. Oh, of course she shouldn't have said anything of the sort, Felicity. But you see people had no etiquette departments in those days. And when the red sunlight of a fair October dawn was shining over the gray sea The Fair Lady sailed out of Charlottetown harbour. On her deck stood Kenneth and Ursula MacNair, and in her hand, as a most precious treasure, the bride carried a ball of gray homespun yarn."

"Well," said Dan, yawning, "I like that kind of a story. Nobody goes and dies in it, that's one good thing."

"Did old Hugh forgive Ursula?" I asked.

"The story stopped there in the brown book," said the Story Girl, "but the Awkward Man says he did, after awhile."

"It must be rather romantic to be run away with," remarked Cecily, wistfully.

"Don't you get such silly notions in your head, Cecily King," said Felicity, severely.

Rewrite this passage so it reads like a human wrote it:
I came to an abrupt halt, momentarily stunned by the breathtaking view of a sunlit clearing that unfolded before me. This seemingly unremarkable glade, cradled within the expansive embrace of a colossal tree trunk, pulsed with life—its soil bustling with vibrant seedlings audaciously taking root in the freshly disturbed earth. Beyond this serene sanctuary, the forest thrummed with energy, a rich tapestry of twisting vines, towering trunks, and bursts of luminous fungi and wildflowers. Nestled among the decaying remnants of the ancient tree, three bizarre figures were engaged in animated conversation, completely oblivious to my presence. One of them, a woman, stood prominently between two distinctly male companions. Their bodies were adorned in ragged strips of crimson fabric, awkwardly draping around their waists, and their skin manifested an unsettling shade of pinkish-brown, unlike anyone I had ever encountered during my wanderings. Their faces formed a grotesque tableau of heavy jowls, receding hairlines, and tufts of wiry hair struggling for dominance on their scalps. These peculiar beings transcended the boundaries of my imagination.

Captivated by their lively dialogue, one man spoke with fervor, his passionate voice seizing the attention of his companions, who remained blissfully unaware of the gentle rustling of leaves that marked my approach. They nodded in perfect synchrony, their movements mirroring the cadence of his weighty, unintelligible speech—a cryptic riddle shrouded in obscurity. As his voice escalated, he thrust his arm skyward and jumped to his feet; his companions mirrored his actions, creating a dissonant chorus as they swayed in unison to the rhythm of their chant. I couldn't help but notice the strange, stubby proportions of their legs and the awkwardness of their movements. Gradually, they began to encircle one another, stomping and flailing in a bewildering dance; from their chaotic motions emerged a melodic refrain echoing phrases like “Aloola” or “Balloola.” Their eyes sparkled with a disquieting intensity, and their distorted features emanated a joy that was both strange and intoxicating, pools of saliva collecting at their lipless mouths.

As I watched their enigmatic performance unfold, the source of my unease crystallized: these figures, despite their vaguely human semblance, bore an uncanny resemblance to wild animals. Each one, whether through their humanoid appearance or ragged clothing, exuded a primal essence, evident in their movements, expressions, and overall demeanor—a striking corpulence that unmistakably branded them as creatures of the wild.

Frozen by this unsettling realization, I was swept into a torrent of disturbing questions. In a sudden surge of energy, they erupted into jubilant leaps, grunting and whooping in a frenzied display until one stumbled, briefly dropping to all fours before springing back up with surprising agility. That fleeting glimpse into their untamed nature sent an electrifying shiver racing down my spine.

With a heavy heart, I turned away, acutely aware of every snap of twigs and swish of leaves that might betray my presence, retreating deeper into the underbrush. I paused at the faintest sound, cautiously retracing my steps. It felt like an eternity before I found the courage to move freely once again. All I craved was to escape the clutches of those grotesque figures, and soon I stumbled upon a faint path winding through the trees. Just then, passing through another small glade, I caught sight of two awkward legs stealthily navigating the woods, no more than thirty yards ahead. The creature's torso and head were concealed behind a curtain of vines. I froze, fervently hoping it remained unaware of my presence. As I stilled, it too paused. I fought the instinct to flee, straining to peer through the dense foliage until the features of the creature I had glimpsed began to sharpen into focus. It shifted slightly, and for a fleeting moment, an emerald glint caught the light in its eyes as it regarded me from the shadows before that brightness faded as it turned away. It lingered for a heartbeat, then vanished swiftly into the densely woven underbrush behind a tangle of brambles. Even after its departure, the unsettling sensation of its gaze persisted—watchful and lingering.

What was this creature—a man or a beast? What did it seek from me? I bore no weapon for defense, not even a simple branch. To flee would be madness. Yet, it showed no inclination to attack. Clenching my jaw, I resolved to forge ahead, striving to mask the paralyzing fear gnawing at my spine. As I pushed through a thicket of tall, white-flowering bushes, I saw it once more about twenty paces ahead, glancing back over its shoulder, caught in a moment of uncertainty. Gradually, I closed the distance, locking eyes with it.

“Who are you?” I called out, my voice steady despite the tremors churning within.

It struggled to meet my gaze. “No!” it exclaimed suddenly, and in an instant, it bolted into the underbrush. Yet, it hesitated again, turning back to fix its fierce gaze upon me from the shadows beneath the trees, its eyes flickering with a wild intensity.

My heart raced, but I realized my only hope lay in maintaining a semblance of calm; thus, I continued my advance with deliberate steps. Once again, it turned and melted into the dim twilight. I thought I caught another flicker of its eyes, and then—it was gone.

I stopped just in time to prevent myself emerging upon an open space. It was a kind of glade in the forest, made by a fall; seedlings were already starting up to struggle for the vacant space; and beyond, the dense growth of stems and twining vines and splashes of fungus and flowers closed in again. Before me, squatting together upon the fungoid ruins of a huge fallen tree and still unaware of my approach, were three grotesque human figures. One was evidently a female; the other two were men. They were naked, save for swathings of scarlet cloth about the middle; and their skins were of a dull pinkish-drab colour, such as I had seen in no savages before. They had fat, heavy, chinless faces, retreating foreheads, and a scant bristly hair upon their heads. I never saw such bestial-looking creatures.


They were talking, or at least one of the men was talking to the other two, and all three had been too closely interested to heed the rustling of my approach. They swayed their heads and shoulders from side to side. The speaker’s words came thick and sloppy, and though I could hear them distinctly I could not distinguish what he said. He seemed to me to be reciting some complicated gibberish. Presently his articulation became shriller, and spreading his hands he rose to his feet. At that the others began to gibber in unison, also rising to their feet, spreading their hands and swaying their bodies in rhythm with their chant. I noticed then the abnormal shortness of their legs, and their lank, clumsy feet. All three began slowly to circle round, raising and stamping their feet and waving their arms; a kind of tune crept into their rhythmic recitation, and a refrain,—“Aloola,” or “Balloola,” it sounded like. Their eyes began to sparkle, and their ugly faces to brighten, with an expression of strange pleasure. Saliva dripped from their lipless mouths.


Suddenly, as I watched their grotesque and unaccountable gestures, I perceived clearly for the first time what it was that had offended me, what had given me the two inconsistent and conflicting impressions of utter strangeness and yet of the strangest familiarity. The three creatures engaged in this mysterious rite were human in shape, and yet human beings with the strangest air about them of some familiar animal. Each of these creatures, despite its human form, its rag of clothing, and the rough humanity of its bodily form, had woven into it—into its movements, into the expression of its countenance, into its whole presence—some now irresistible suggestion of a hog, a swinish taint, the unmistakable mark of the beast.

At the center of the gathering, Mr. Standish commanded the room with an unmistakable air of authority. He cleared his throat deliberately, capturing the complete attention of everyone present. "What I have to share with you today," he began, his voice rich with sincerity, "is a will meticulously composed by my own hand and officially approved by our dearly departed friend on August 9, 1825. Yet, I have stumbled upon another document, one that has remained unknown to me until now. Dated July 20, 1826, it emerges nearly a year later. Furthermore," he continued, adjusting his glasses with care, "there is an accompanying codicil dated March 1, 1828."

"My goodness!" Sister Martha gasped, the gravity of the revelation weighing heavily on her heart.

"I will commence by reading the original will," Mr. Standish declared, his resolve unwavering. "The mere existence of this document suggests that the deceased intended for it to endure through time."

As he began to read, the preamble seemed to stretch on endlessly, stirring restlessness among some attendees, who eventually released a collective sigh of resignation. Solomon shook his head slowly, his eyes cast down, while others were drawn into the intricate designs of the tablecloth or the gleaming surface of Mr. Standish’s bald head. The lone exception was Mary Garth, who felt an unexpected rush of bravery as the events unfolded. The moment Mr. Standish articulated the phrase "give and bequeath," a palpable shift coursed through the room, sparking varied reactions—except for Mr. Rigg, whose unflappable demeanor stood in stark contrast to the growing tension. Attention turned to the implications of the bequests, momentarily diverting thoughts from him. Fred's face flushed with anxiety, while Mr. Vincy nervously toyed with his snuffbox, clenching it tightly despite its firmly closed lid.

The will began with small bequests, amplifying the suspense surrounding the rumored existence of a second will and the unsettling possibility that Peter’s affections had shifted. A lingering desire for fair distribution permeated the assembly, weighed down by echoes of history, present circumstances, and looming future outcomes. Just five years prior, Peter had allocated a mere two hundred pounds to each of his siblings and a paltry hundred to his nephews and nieces. Notably, the Garths were glaringly omitted from his will, while Mrs. Vincy and Rosamond each received a hundred pounds. Mr. Trumbull was bequeathed a gold-headed cane and fifty pounds, while other cousins received trivial sums that, as Mr. Trumbull lamented, served no real purpose. Numerous other meager legacies were designated for absent relatives or dubious acquaintances. As the onlookers tallied the distributions, it became clear that just over three thousand pounds had been allocated. Where, then, would the remaining fortune be directed? What fate awaited the estate? Which bequests had been revoked, and which endured—would such alterations serve as solace or merely deepen the discontent? Each flicker of emotion was shrouded in a haze of suspicion. The men maintained a facade of composure; some allowed their lips to droop in resignation while others pressed them together tightly, a silent proclamation of their unease. In stark contrast, Jane and Martha were swept away by emotion, tears glistening in their eyes; Mrs. Cranch felt torn between gratitude for her modest inheritance and a lingering sense of inadequacy. Meanwhile, Mrs. Waule wrestled with bitterness, feeling justly aggrieved by her meager portion while others stood to gain significantly. The prevailing assumption was that Fred Vincy would inherit the largest share. To the shock of the Vincys, the announcement of a ten-thousand-pound bequest designated for specific investments rippled through the room, raising the question—would the land accompany it? Fred bit his lip, struggling to repress a burgeoning smile as Mrs. Vincy beamed with delight, the specter of potential revocation fading in the glow of such hopeful prospects.

Yet a considerable range of personal assets remained untouched, all allocated to a single beneficiary—oh, the tantalizing enigma! Oh, the lofty hopes we place on the affections of "close" elderly gentlemen! Oh, the unrestrained sentiments vying to capture the absurdities of human expectations! Strangely, the sole remaining heir was none other than Joshua Rigg, who also served as executor, inheriting the esteemed Featherstone title.

A tangible tremor rippled through the assembly as a wave of anticipatory rustling swept over them. Every gaze converged again on Mr. Rigg, whose expression remained inscrutable.

"What an astonishing testament this will is!" Mr. Trumbull interjected, momentarily shedding his usual air of sagacity. "However, we face the pressing matter of a second will—a document entirely different in nature. We have yet to uncover the full intentions of the deceased."

Mary Garth suspected that any concealed truths woven into this affair stretched far beyond the documents before them. The second will would nullify everything except the modest legacies (with specific conditions activating the codicil), including a bequest of all land within the Lowick parish, along with stocks and household furnishings, to Joshua Rigg. The remainder of the estate was to be committed to establishing almshouses for elderly men, to be named Featherstone's Almshouses, constructed on a tract of land near Middlemarch that the testator had purposefully acquired for this noble cause, driven by a desire to honor God. None present would leave with a single penny; yet Mr. Trumbull clutched the gold-headed cane, an incongruent sight. The assembly took considerable time to pull their thoughts into any semblance of clarity. Mary dared not meet Fred’s gaze.

It was Mr. Vincy who first broke the silence, anxiously toying with his snuffbox. His frustration crackled through the room: "The most bewildering will I’ve ever encountered! One can only assume he was not of sound mind when he devised it. I declare this last will to be invalid," he proclaimed, convinced he grasped the crux of the matter. "Do you not agree, Standish?"

"I am steadfast in my belief that our late friend was fully aware of his intentions," Mr. Standish replied, his tone unwavering and composed. "Everything appears to be in proper order. Here is a letter from Clemens of Brassing, securely attached to the will. He is the one who drafted it—an esteemed solicitor."

"I never observed any signs of confusion or impaired judgment in the late Mr. Featherstone," Borthrop Trumbull declared. "Nonetheless, this will strikes me as peculiar. I had always been at the service of that old gentleman, and he made it abundantly clear that he felt a duty to articulate his wishes in writing. The gold-headed cane hardly acknowledges my contributions; fortunately, I possess values far beyond mere financial reward."

"Honestly, I find nothing particularly shocking about this situation," Caleb Garth remarked. "One would have been more astonished if the will conformed to the expectations of a straightforward individual. Personally, I yearn for a world free from the burdens imposed by wills."

"The will I hold in my hand," said Mr. Standish, who, seated at the table in the middle of the room, took his time about everything, including the coughs with which he showed a disposition to clear his voice, "was drawn up by myself and executed by our deceased friend on the 9th of August, 1825. But I find that there is a subsequent instrument hitherto unknown to me, bearing date the 20th of July, 1826, hardly a year later than the previous one. And there is farther, I see"--Mr. Standish was cautiously travelling over the document with his spectacles--"a codicil to this latter will, bearing date March 1, 1828."

"Dear, dear!" said sister Martha, not meaning to be audible, but driven to some articulation under this pressure of dates.

"I shall begin by reading the earlier will," continued Mr. Standish, "since such, as appears by his not having destroyed the document, was the intention of deceased."

The preamble was felt to be rather long, and several besides Solomon shook their heads pathetically, looking on the ground: all eyes avoided meeting other eyes, and were chiefly fixed either on the spots in the table-cloth or on Mr. Standish's bald head; excepting Mary Garth's. When all the rest were trying to look nowhere in particular, it was safe for her to look at them. And at the sound of the first "give and bequeath" she could see all complexions changing subtly, as if some faint vibration were passing through them, save that of Mr. Rigg. He sat in unaltered calm, and, in fact, the company, preoccupied with more important problems, and with the complication of listening to bequests which might or might not be revoked, had ceased to think of him. Fred blushed, and Mr. Vincy found it impossible to do without his snuff-box in his hand, though he kept it closed.

The small bequests came first, and even the recollection that there was another will and that poor Peter might have thought better of it, could not quell the rising disgust and indignation. One likes to be done well by in every tense, past, present, and future. And here was Peter capable five years ago of leaving only two hundred apiece to his own brothers and sisters, and only a hundred apiece to his own nephews and nieces: the Garths were not mentioned, but Mrs. Vincy and Rosamond were each to have a hundred. Mr. Trumbull was to have the gold-headed cane and fifty pounds; the other second cousins and the cousins present were each to have the like handsome sum, which, as the saturnine cousin observed, was a sort of legacy that left a man nowhere; and there was much more of such offensive dribbling in favor of persons not present--problematical, and, it was to be feared, low connections. Altogether, reckoning hastily, here were about three thousand disposed of. Where then had Peter meant the rest of the money to go--and where the land? and what was revoked and what not revoked--and was the revocation for better or for worse? All emotion must be conditional, and might turn out to be the wrong thing. The men were strong enough to bear up and keep quiet under this confused suspense; some letting their lower lip fall, others pursing it up, according to the habit of their muscles. But Jane and Martha sank under the rush of questions, and began to cry; poor Mrs. Cranch being half moved with the consolation of getting any hundreds at all without working for them, and half aware that her share was scanty; whereas Mrs. Waule's mind was entirely flooded with the sense of being an own sister and getting little, while somebody else was to have much. The general expectation now was that the "much" would fall to Fred Vincy, but the Vincys themselves were surprised when ten thousand pounds in specified investments were declared to be bequeathed to him:--was the land coming too? Fred bit his lips: it was difficult to help smiling, and Mrs. Vincy felt herself the happiest of women--possible revocation shrinking out of sight in this dazzling vision.

There was still a residue of personal property as well as the land, but the whole was left to one person, and that person was--O possibilities! O expectations founded on the favor of "close" old gentlemen! O endless vocatives that would still leave expression slipping helpless from the measurement of mortal folly!--that residuary legatee was Joshua Rigg, who was also sole executor, and who was to take thenceforth the name of Featherstone.

There was a rustling which seemed like a shudder running round the room. Every one stared afresh at Mr. Rigg, who apparently experienced no surprise.

"A most singular testamentary disposition!" exclaimed Mr. Trumbull, preferring for once that he should be considered ignorant in the past. "But there is a second will--there is a further document. We have not yet heard the final wishes of the deceased."

Mary Garth was feeling that what they had yet to hear were not the final wishes. The second will revoked everything except the legacies to the low persons before mentioned (some alterations in these being the occasion of the codicil), and the bequest of all the land lying in Lowick parish with all the stock and household furniture, to Joshua Rigg. The residue of the property was to be devoted to the erection and endowment of almshouses for old men, to be called Featherstone's Alms-Houses, and to be built on a piece of land near Middlemarch already bought for the purpose by the testator, he wishing--so the document declared--to please God Almighty. Nobody present had a farthing; but Mr. Trumbull had the gold-headed cane. It took some time for the company to recover the power of expression. Mary dared not look at Fred.

Mr. Vincy was the first to speak--after using his snuff-box energetically--and he spoke with loud indignation. "The most unaccountable will I ever heard! I should say he was not in his right mind when he made it. I should say this last will was void," added Mr. Vincy, feeling that this expression put the thing in the true light. "Eh Standish?"

"Our deceased friend always knew what he was about, I think," said Mr. Standish. "Everything is quite regular. Here is a letter from Clemens of Brassing tied with the will. He drew it up. A very respectable solicitor."

"I never noticed any alienation of mind--any aberration of intellect in the late Mr. Featherstone," said Borthrop Trumbull, "but I call this will eccentric. I was always willingly of service to the old soul; and he intimated pretty plainly a sense of obligation which would show itself in his will. The gold-headed cane is farcical considered as an acknowledgment to me; but happily I am above mercenary considerations."

"There's nothing very surprising in the matter that I can see," said Caleb Garth. "Anybody might have had more reason for wondering if the will had been what you might expect from an open-minded straightforward man. For my part, I wish there was no such thing as a will."

These worthies looked strangely like bad angels, or at least like men who had wrestled so continually and so sternly with the Devil that somewhat of his sooty fierceness had been imparted to their own visages. They had all vanished now; a cheerful coat of paint and golden-tinted paper-hangings lighted up the small apartment; while the shadow of a willow-tree that swept against the overhanging eaves atempered the cheery western sunshine. It never has a vivacious aspect, except when a northwestern breeze is vexing its surface on a sunshiny day. Flags and rushes grow along its plashy shore; the yellow water-lily spreads its broad, flat leaves on the margin; and the fragrant white pond-lily abounds, generally selecting a position just so far from the river’s brink that it cannot be grasped save at the hazard of plunging in.


It is a marvel whence this perfect flower derives its loveliness and perfume, springing as it does from the black mud over which the river sleeps, and where lurk the slimy eel, and speckled frog, and the mud-turtle, whom continual washing cannot cleanse. It is the very same black mud out of which the yellow lily sucks its obscene life and noisome odor. Thus we see, too, in the world that some persons assimilate only what is ugly and evil from the same moral circumstances which supply good and beautiful results—the fragrance of celestial flowers—to the daily life of others.


The reader must not, from any testimony of mine, contract a dislike towards our slumberous stream. Each tree and rock and every blade of grass is distinctly imaged, and, however unsightly in reality, assumes ideal beauty in the reflection. The minutest things of earth and the broad aspect of the firmament are pictured equally without effort and with the same felicity of success. With shaking hands, she handed him the letter, her body taut as she watched him read. The moment he recognized the familiar handwriting of Evadne, the color drained from his face. In that fleeting instant, the gravity of their situation hit him; their world teetered on the brink of catastrophe. Any residual doubts about deceit evaporated under the heavy weight of their crisis. He understood that he had to either allay Perdita’s fears or risk losing her forever. “My sweetest,” he began earnestly, “I have faltered; please forgive me. Perdita gasped, urging him to continue. “What more needs to be said? Speak plainly!”

“That is everything I can share,” he replied solemnly. “This letter uncovers it all. I have become entangled in a troubling situation. I thought I could manage it, but perhaps I have erred. Regardless, my love for you remains steadfast.”

Perdita shook her head in disbelief. “That cannot be the case,” she declared defiantly. “I see through your facade. You are trying to mislead me, but I refuse to be deceived. I feel you slipping away from me, and losing you would mean losing my very self—my essence!”

“Do you truly doubt my words?” Raymond asked, incredulity tainting his voice.

“To trust you,” she replied, her voice rising, “would mean surrendering everything, and I would choose death over the agony of betrayal—but I can hardly endure this torment!”

“Perdita,” he implored earnestly, “you do not grasp the fragility of your position. I didn’t choose this path lightly; I knew my silence could evoke your suspicions. Yet, I hoped my reassurances would put your mind at ease. Do you really believe I would disregard my truths? I refuse to be diminished; my honor remains intact. You have loved me, and I have reciprocated that love. Yet even the strongest emotions can fade over time. Let our love develop, but do not allow it to plunge into mistrust or blame. Until now, we have cherished a bond rooted in both passion and friendship—let us not become adversaries. I cannot thrive in an atmosphere of doubt. If you cannot trust me, then perhaps it would be best for us to separate.”

“Exactly,” Perdita retorted, her voice rising. “I feared this outcome! Are we not already apart? Is there not a chasm wider than the ocean between us?”

Raymond stood, his voice shaky yet unnaturally calm, reminiscent of a haunting stillness before a storm. “I find an odd comfort in your acceptance of my choice. Surely, you will wear the mantle of the victim with ease. Occasionally, you may grapple with the notion that you have wronged me, but the sympathy of your family, society’s pity, and the façade of your innocence will cushion your fall—I vow never to cross your path again.”

He turned toward the door, oblivious to the deception woven into his every word. He donned a mask of innocence while teetering on the edge of self-delusion. Just as actors weep for stories fabricated, Raymond felt reality mingling with his pretense. His words dripped with arrogance, fueled by his own grievances. Perdita perceived the flicker of defiance in his eyes as his hand hovered over the door’s lock. Her head rested against his shoulder, trembling as warmth and cold raced through her. Observing her distress, he softened his tone.

Faith and loyalty have forged our connection; if we forsake that, what reason do we have to cling to the fragments of a hollow existence? You have your child, your brother—Idris, Adrian—”

“And you,” Perdita interjected, “you who wrote that letter.”

A storm of indignation flashed in Raymond's eyes, recognizing the folly of her accusation. “Cling to that notion if you must,” he snapped back, “make it your fortress, a balm for your restless mind—so be it. Perdita felt the impact of his fierce words. “I do not deny your truth, Raymond; quite the opposite. I promise to place my trust in you wholeheartedly. “I have already confirmed my loyalty,” he replied coldly, “but repeated reassurances lose their meaning without your trust. I can offer no further proof of what you have already rejected. This argument is unworthy of us both, and I admit I am weary of discussing unfounded, unkind accusations.”

Perdita sought his gaze, but he turned away in anger. Yet, the authenticity of his ire quelled her doubts. A flicker of love reignited within him. However, mending the rift with Raymond would not be an easy task. Initially, he resisted her attempts at reconciliation, but her determination remained unyielding. Confident in his enduring affection, she was willing to express any humble plea necessary to earn his forgiveness. Gradually, she captured his attention; he sat in thoughtful silence while still listening intently. She began by pledging her unwavering faith—he needed to understand that without it, she would not strive to keep him close.

She summoned memories of their shared happiness, painting a vivid picture of their future together while speaking of their child. Tears sprang to her eyes unexpectedly, and despite her best efforts to hold them back, they overflowed—her voice shaking. It had been years since she last cried. Raymond could not bear to witness her raw grief; a wave of guilt surged through him for portraying himself as the wronged party when he was, in truth, the architect of her torment. His love for Perdita surged; her tender spirit, the golden cascade of her hair, the gentle curve of her form—all ignited profound tenderness and admiration within him. He comforted her with gentle words and gestures, allowing himself to believe that, in that moment, wrapped in her warmth, he had never truly wronged her at all.

The perfect confidence that subsisted between Perdita and him, rendered every communication common between them. They opened each other's letters, even as, until now, the inmost fold of the heart of each was disclosed to the other. A letter came unawares, Perdita read it. Had it contained confirmation, she must have been annihilated. As it was, trembling, cold, and pale, she sought Raymond. He was alone, examining some petitions lately presented. She entered silently, sat on a sofa opposite to him, and gazed on him with a look of such despair, that wildest shrieks and dire moans would have been tame exhibitions of misery, compared to the living incarnation of the thing itself exhibited by her.

At first he did not take his eyes from the papers; when he raised them, he was struck by the wretchedness manifest on her altered cheek; for a moment he forgot his own acts and fears, and asked with consternation--"Dearest girl, what is the matter; what has happened?"

"Nothing," she replied at first; "and yet not so," she continued, hurrying on in her speech; "you have secrets, Raymond; where have you been lately, whom have you seen, what do you conceal from me?--why am I banished from your confidence? Yet this is not it--I do not intend to entrap you with questions--one will suffice--am I completely a wretch?"

With trembling hand she gave him the paper, and sat white and motionless looking at him while he read it. He recognised the hand-writing of Evadne, and the colour mounted in his cheeks. With lightning-speed he conceived the contents of the letter; all was now cast on one die; falsehood and artifice were trifles in comparison with the impending ruin. He would either entirely dispel Perdita's suspicions, or quit her for ever. "My dear girl," he said, "I have been to blame; but you must pardon me.
