“Tom, we must hurry to the station!” Fanny insisted, her voice quivering with urgency.  
“Let’s not waste any more time,” he retorted sharply, his annoyance sharpening his tone.  
“Are you serious? It’s absolutely pouring outside! I’d feel utterly foolish stepping into that downpour—I prefer to make a grand entrance when Polly arrives,” she elaborated, irritation flickering across her features like lightning.  
“Do you expect me to fetch a complete stranger by myself?” Tom protested, panic manifesting on his face, as if he were gearing up for a daring expedition with a reckless sidekick.  
“Of course you can! It’s your duty to bring her here. Besides, who knows? If you weren’t being such a killjoy, you might even enjoy it,” she shot back, her annoyance softening with the hint of a playful grin.  
“That’s incredibly unfair! I thought we were in this together; you promised to come with me! There’s no way I’m facing one of your friends alone!” With that, Tom sprang from the sofa, indignation radiating from him, though his wild hair and mismatched clothing undermined the gravity of his protest.  
“Stop being so negative! I’ll charm Mama into allowing you to invite that tiresome Ned Miller after Polly leaves,” Fanny replied, her tone sweetening in an attempt to soothe him.  
“How long will she be staying?” Tom asked, giving himself a half-hearted shake, trying to appear somewhat presentable despite his embarrassment.  
“Probably a month or two. She’s absolutely delightful, and I’ll make certain she stays as long as she's happy.”  
“She won't stick around for long if I can help it,” Tom muttered, the typical disdain of a fourteen-year-old rising to the surface as he dismissed girls as mere bothersome annoyances. Such fleeting musings danced through the mind of a boy—an escape that offered careless amusement before devolving into the frustrating realities of “those irritating girls.”  
“Wait! How will I even recognize her? I’ve never met her, and she hasn't met me! You have to come with me, Fanny!” he pleaded, reaching for the door, suddenly daunted by the prospect of navigating through a crowd of unfamiliar girls in search of the right one.  
“You’ll be able to spot her; she’ll likely be scanning the crowd for us. I’m sure she’ll recognize you from everything I’ve told her,” Fanny reassured him.  
“I highly doubt it,” Tom replied, running a distracted hand through his curls as he studied his reflection, unconvinced that his sister had accurately conveyed his appeal. Sisters have a talent for misrepresenting the truth—“we fellows” know that well enough.  
“Hurry up, or you’ll be late! What will Polly think of me?” Fanny exclaimed, nudging him in exasperation, a gesture that stung Tom's pride.  
“She’ll probably think you care more about appearances than about your friends, and honestly, she wouldn’t be wrong.” Satisfied with his clever retort, Tom ambled away nonchalantly, acutely aware of the ticking clock yet determined to savor the moment, fully intending to make a dash at the last second.  
“If I were president, I would pass a law silencing all boys until they mature; they truly are the most unbearable creatures,” Fanny mused, watching her brother's slumped figure blur down the street. Yet her perspective might have shifted had she followed him, for the moment he turned the corner, his demeanor transformed entirely. His hands slipped from his pockets, his whistling faded, he smoothed his jacket and adjusted his cap, marching forth with newfound resolve.  

Tom arrived at the station just as the train rolled in, breathless and flushed from the brisk wind and exertion.  
“I wonder if she'll show up in some elaborate gown with a complicated hairstyle like the others; how will I know it’s her? It’s so unfair that Fanny made me come here alone!” he fretted, scanning the bustling crowd, utterly overwhelmed by the swarm of young ladies flitting past. None appeared to be waiting for anyone in particular, leading to his hesitation, his expression resigned to the chaos. “That must be her,” he thought, spotting a girl in a striking outfit, her hands clasped and a delicate hat nestled atop an elaborate chignon. “I suppose I must say something; here goes,” he steeled himself, summoning his courage as he approached the stylish stranger, her attire fluttering in the wind, ribbons dancing around her.  
“Excuse me, are you Polly Milton?” Tom ventured tentatively, positioning himself before the chic young lady.  
“No, I’m not,” she replied coolly, immediately deflating his confidence.  
“Where on earth can she be?” Tom grumbled, irritation creeping in as he turned away. Just then, he heard the rapid patter of footsteps behind him and turned to see a bright-eyed little girl hurrying down the long station aisle, her face aglow with joy. Beaming and waving at him with her bag, he hesitated, wondering, “Could that be Polly?”  
The little girl bounded over, extending her hand, a mix of shyness and excitement lighting up her blue eyes. “Are you Tom?” she asked.  
“Yes. How did you know?” Tom replied, surprised yet shaking her hand with genuine enthusiasm.  
“Oh, Fanny told me all about you! She mentioned you had curly hair, a quirky nose, and that you were always whistling. Plus, you wore a gray cap pulled low, so I recognized you right away.” Polly smiled, cleverly bypassing the less flattering descriptors of “red,” “pug,” and “old” that Fanny may have included.  
“Where are your trunks?” Tom asked, suddenly recalling his duty as she handed him her bag—one he hadn’t even offered to carry.  
“Father told me not to wait for anyone or I’d miss my cab, so I gave my check to a man, and there he is with my trunk.” Polly began walking toward her modest piece of luggage, Tom trailing closely behind, feeling a twinge of guilt for neglecting his manners. “Thank goodness she’s not like the typical young ladies!” he thought. “Fanny never mentioned she was attractive. She’s nothing like the city girls and doesn’t behave like them either.”  

As the carriage rolled away, Polly hopped into the bouncy seat, erupting in laughter like a carefree child. “I absolutely adore these delightful carriages, soaking in all the sights and having an incredible time, don’t you?” she exclaimed, momentarily redoubling her efforts to maintain her composure.  
“Not really,” Tom replied absentmindedly, sensing the weight of confinement in a carriage with a stranger settling heavily upon him.  
“How’s Fanny? Why didn’t she come with you?” Polly inquired, her eyes sparkling with excitement despite her attempts at decorum.  
“She was worried about ruining her curls,” Tom chuckled, boyish pride swelling as he acknowledged the unintended compliment he had just delivered.  
“You and I don’t mind a little rain. Thank you for looking after me.”  
Polly’s genuine appreciation melted Tom's defenses, and he found himself valuing her kindness, even though he had only carried her bag for a few steps. Feeling generous, he rummaged through the snack-filled pockets of his trousers, producing a handful of peanuts, remnants of his usual overindulgence marked by discarded shells.  

The moment he did, he recalled Fanny’s disdain for peanuts and felt a flicker of shame wash over him. Leaning out of the window for too long, Polly finally asked, “Is something wrong?” “Oh, who cares about a country girl like her?” Tom thought boldly, yet mischief began to fester within him.  
“He looks a bit wobbly, but I reckon he can manage the horses,” he joked, adopting an exaggerated air of carefree nonchalance.  
“Is the driver drunk? Oh no! Are the horses out of control? Is it safe?” Polly gasped, concern etched across her face as she adjusted her small beaver hat and glanced nervously out the half-open window.  
“There are plenty of people around to catch us if anything goes wrong. But honestly, it might be safer if I sit with the driver,” Tom suggested cheerfully, relishing the cleverness of his ploy.  
“Oh, please do if you’re not scared! Mother would be so distressed if something happened to me while I’m so far from home!” Polly exclaimed, visibly unsettled.  
“Don’t worry; I’ll take care of the old man and the horses!” Tom declared confidently, swinging the door wide open and leaving the anxious Polly trembling inside as he joyfully embraced the freedom outside, munching on peanuts alongside the driver.

"IT 'S time to go to the station, Tom."
"Come on, then."
"Oh, I 'm not going; it 's too wet. Should n't have a crimp left if I went out such a day as this; and I want to look nice when Polly comes."
"You don't expect me to go and bring home a strange girl alone, do you?" And Tom looked as much alarmed as if his sister had proposed to him to escort the wild woman of Australia.
"Of course I do. It 's your place to go and get her; and if you was n't a bear, you 'd like it."
"Well, I call that mean! I supposed I 'd got to go; but you said you 'd go, too. Catch me bothering about your friends another time! No, sir!" And Tom rose from the sofa with an air of indignant resolution, the impressive effect of which was somewhat damaged by a tousled head, and the hunched appearance of his garments generally.
"Now, don't be cross; and I 'll get mamma to let you have that horrid Ned Miller, that you are so fond of, come and make you a visit after Polly 's gone," said Fanny, hoping to soothe his ruffled feelings.
"How long is she going to stay?" demanded Tom, making his toilet by a promiscuous shake.
"A month or two, maybe. She 's ever so nice; and I shall keep her as long as she 's happy."
"She won't stay long then, if I can help it," muttered Tom, who regarded girls as a very unnecessary portion of creation. Boys of fourteen are apt to think so, and perhaps it is a wise arrangement; for, being fond of turning somersaults, they have an opportunity of indulging in a good one, metaphorically speaking, when, three or four years later, they become the abject slaves of "those bothering girls."
"Look here! how am I going to know the creature? I never saw her, and she never saw me. You 'll have to come too, Fan," he added, pausing on his way to the door, arrested by the awful idea that he might have to address several strange girls before he got the right one.
"You'll find her easy enough; she'll probably be standing round looking for us. I dare say she 'll know you, though I 'm not there, because I 've described you to her."
"Guess she won't, then;" and Tom gave a hasty smooth to his curly pate and a glance at the mirror, feeling sure that his sister had n't done him justice. Sisters never do, as "we fellows" know too well.
"Do go along, or you'll be too late; and then, what will Polly think of me?" cried Fanny, with the impatient poke which is peculiarly aggravating to masculine dignity.
"She 'll think you cared more about your frizzles than your friends, and she 'll be about right, too."
Feeling that he said rather a neat and cutting thing, Tom sauntered leisurely away, perfectly conscious that it was late, but bent on not being hurried while in sight, though he ran himself off his legs to make up for it afterward.
"If I was the President, I 'd make a law to shut up all boys till they were grown; for they certainly are the most provoking toads in the world," said Fanny, as she watched the slouchy figure of her brother strolling down the street. She might have changed her mind, however, if she had followed him, for as soon as he turned the corner, his whole aspect altered; his hands came out of his pockets, he stopped whistling, buttoned his jacket, gave his cap a pull, and went off at a great pace.


The train was just in when he reached the station, panting like a race-horse, and as red as a lobster with the wind and the run.
"Suppose she 'll wear a top-knot and a thingumbob, like every one else; and however shall I know her? Too bad of Fan to make me come alone!" thought Tom, as he stood watching the crowd stream through the depot, and feeling rather daunted at the array of young ladies who passed. As none of them seemed looking for any one, he did not accost them, but eyed each new batch with the air of a martyr. "That 's her," he said to himself, as he presently caught sight of a girl in gorgeous array, standing with her hands folded, and a very small hat perched on the top of a very large "chignon," as Tom pronounced it. "I suppose I 've got to speak to her, so here goes;" and, nerving himself to the task, Tom slowly approached the damsel, who looked as if the wind had blown her clothes into rags, such a flapping of sashes, scallops, ruffles, curls, and feathers was there.
"I say, if you please, is your name Polly Milton?" meekly asked Tom, pausing before the breezy stranger.
"No, it is n't," answered the young lady, with a cool stare that utterly quenched him.
"Where in thunder is she?" growled Tom, walking off in high dudgeon. The quick tap of feet behind him made him turn in time to see a fresh-faced little girl running down the long station, and looking as if she rather liked it. As she smiled, and waved her bag at him, he stopped and waited for her, saying to himself, "Hullo! I wonder if that 's Polly?"
Up came the little girl, with her hand out, and a half-shy, half-merry look in her blue eyes, as she said, inquiringly, "This is Tom, is n't it?"
"Yes. How did you know?" and Tom got over the ordeal of hand-shaking without thinking of it, he was so surprised.
"Oh, Fan told me you 'd got curly hair, and a funny nose, and kept whistling, and wore a gray cap pulled over your eyes; so I knew you directly." And Polly nodded at him in the most friendly manner, having politely refrained from calling the hair "red," the nose "a pug," and the cap "old," all of which facts Fanny had carefully impressed upon her memory.
"Where are your trunks?" asked Tom, as he was reminded of his duty by her handing him the bag, which he had not offered to take.
"Father told me not to wait for any one, else I 'd lose my chance of a hack; so I gave my check to a man, and there he is with my trunk;" and Polly walked off after her one modest piece of baggage, followed by Tom, who felt a trifle depressed by his own remissness in polite attentions. "She is n't a bit of a young lady, thank goodness! Fan did n't tell me she was pretty. Don't look like city girls, nor act like 'em, neither," he thought, trudging in the rear, and eyeing with favor the brown curls bobbing along in front.


As the carriage drove off, Polly gave a little bounce on the springy seat, and laughed like a delighted child. "I do like to ride in these nice hacks, and see all the fine things, and have a good time, don't you?" she said, composing herself the next minute, as if it suddenly occurred to her that she was going a-visiting.
"Not much," said Tom, not minding what he said, for the fact that he was shut up with the strange girl suddenly oppressed his soul.
"How 's Fan? Why did n't she come, too?" asked Polly, trying to look demure, while her eyes danced in spite of her.
"Afraid of spoiling her crinkles;" and Tom smiled, for this base betrayal of confidence made him feel his own man again.
"You and I don't mind dampness. I 'm much obliged to you for coming to take care of me."
It was kind of Polly to say that, and Tom felt it; for his red crop was a tender point, and to be associated with Polly's pretty brown curls seemed to lessen its coppery glow. Then he had n't done anything for her but carry the bag a few steps; yet, she thanked him. He felt grateful, and in a burst of confidence, offered a handful of peanuts, for his pockets were always supplied with this agreeable delicacy, and he might be traced anywhere by the trail of shells he left behind him.


As soon as he had done it, he remembered that Fanny considered them vulgar, and felt that he had disgraced his family. So he stuck his head out of the window, and kept it there so long, that Polly asked if anything was the matter. "Pooh! who cares for a countrified little thing like her," said Tom manfully to himself; and then the spirit of mischief entered in and took possession of him.
"He 's pretty drunk; but I guess he can hold his horses," replied this evil-minded boy, with an air of calm resignation.
"Is the man tipsy? Oh, dear! let 's get out! Are the horses bad? It 's very steep here; do you think it 's safe?" cried poor Polly, making a cocked hat of her little beaver, by thrusting it out of the half-open window on her side.
"There 's plenty of folks to pick us up if anything happens; but perhaps it would be safer if I got out and sat with the man;" and Tom quite beamed with the brilliancy of this sudden mode of relief.
"Oh, do, if you ain't afraid! Mother would be so anxious if anything should happen to me, so far away!" cried Polly, much distressed.
"Don't you be worried. I 'll manage the old chap, and the horses too;" and opening the door, Tom vanished aloft, leaving poor victimized Polly to quake inside, while he placidly revelled in freedom and peanuts outside, with the staid old driver.

Rewrite this AI passage to sound more humanlike:
Engulfed in the weight of the formidable challenges before him, Pemberton steeled himself to face them head-on, finding solace in the bond of friendship he held dear. With a refreshingly whimsical take on the dire realities of their situation, Morgan candidly revealed the layers of their struggles, his captivating dialogue so riveting that the thought of retreating into obscurity was utterly alien. Their honest exchanges liberated them from the burden of concealing their true emotions, and this straightforward honesty deepened the connection they shared. In that moment, Morgan shone with a unique radiance, his vulnerabilities gently illuminated by the glow of their mutual trust. What fascinated Pemberton most was the profound pride that emanated from Morgan—a delicate blend of tenderness and strength. He recognized a flicker of that same pride within himself, acutely aware that it would come with its own scars. He yearned for his family to embody a spirit of resilience, bravely confronting the humbling truths that confronted them. While his mother grappled with a debilitating sense of shame, it was his father who bore the heaviest loads. Morgan suggested that Ulick had artfully sidestepped an impending scandal in Nice, masking the family’s troubles behind an elaborate façade of illness too intricate to articulate. Enveloped in a romantic idealism reminiscent of poets and historians, Morgan humorously envisioned that his relatives—whom he playfully chided Pemberton for idolizing—would leave a lasting mark on the world. Yet, it appeared their primary intention was to woo those who barely acknowledged their existence, flaunting social rebuffs like medals of honor. The reasons behind their social unpopularity baffled him; they were far from unattractive. In truth, their intellect surpassed the superficiality of the empty aristocrats they chased across Europe in search of validation. “In the end, they do put on quite the show, don’t they?” he pondered, embodying an air of ancient wisdom. Without missing a beat, Pemberton replied, “The esteemed Moreen family? An undeniable source of entertainment! Had our unfortunate interruption—ah, those poor actors—not occurred, they might have made an unforgettable impression!”

What weighed heaviest on Pemberton was the erratic and seemingly arbitrary nature of their social disgrace, which clashed painfully with his sense of self-worth. While individuals can steer their own destinies, why had his family chosen a path fraught with flattery, deceit, and manipulation? What grave misdeeds had their ancestors—whom he still held in high regard—committed to deserve such a tarnished legacy? What unwitting sins had he committed to inherit a family history marred by a timid yearning for societal approval, especially when such pursuits promised only humiliation? Their aspirations were glaringly transparent, and it was this very openness that repelled the very people they longed to impress. There was neither dignity nor semblance of shame in their interactions; pride was absent, as well as bitterness or any trace of disgust. If only his father or brother would find the courage to confront someone—what calamity could possibly arise from engaging in a minor quarrel once or twice a year? Despite their undeniable intelligence, they remained blissfully unaware of the impressions they left behind. Indeed, they were amiable—amiable like shopkeepers welcoming customers! But was this the legacy he envisioned for his family? Morgan recalled a grandfather from New York whom he cherished from his youth. This distinguished gentleman, adorned in a high neckcloth and armed with an impressive vocabulary, wore a morning coat that sparked intrigue regarding his evening attire; he was rumored to possess wealth and a connection to the Bible Society. Without question, he epitomized dignity. Pemberton remembered Mrs. Clancy, the widowed sister of Mr. Moreen, who embodied the very frustration of a moral lesson and had made a fleeting visit to the family in Nice shortly after his arrival. “Pure and refined,” Amy would croon to the melody of a banjo, exuding an air of cryptic wisdom as if guarding some essential truth. Pemberton speculated that her silence stemmed from an unspoken endorsement of many family traditions; it could be assumed she too hailed from a respectable lineage and that Mr. and Mrs. Moreen, along with Ulick, Paula, and Amy, could effortlessly claim a superior status if they wished.

Yet, their reluctance to claim that status grew ever more evident. They remained ensnared in their “chivey,” as Morgan astutely termed it, devising endless rationalizations for a trip to Venice. Their reasons were abundant—always refreshingly sincere; they engaged in spirited debates over leisurely breakfasts while the women prepared, elbows resting on the table and deliberating on what they “truly ought” to do, effortlessly switching to languages that facilitated more authentic expression. Even Pemberton found himself increasingly forgiving toward Ulick in those moments, especially when Ulick’s monotone voice intoned, “the sweet sea-city.” This sparked a flicker of affection within him—their carefree detachment from the mundane made Pemberton feel equally unmoored. As summer waned and laughter filled the air, they gathered on the balcony overlooking the Grand Canal. The sunsets were nothing short of breathtaking, and finally, the Dorringtons made their long-awaited appearance. Their absence from breakfast conversations had been glaring, even as unspoken topics hovered around. However, the Dorringtons’ visits were rare; when their presence graced the gathering, they lingered for hours, naturally. During these times, Mrs. Moreen and the girls frequently checked in at their hotel—sometimes even making three visits in quick succession—eager to see if they had returned. The gondola was reserved for the women, as Venice dictated “days,” a lesson Mrs. Moreen quickly grasped upon her arrival. She promptly arranged one for herself, although the Dorringtons often chose not to join her. On one occasion, Pemberton and his companion strolled through St. Mark's—having savored their finest adventures and spent ample time exploring various churches—they observed the elderly lord entering with Mr. Moreen and Ulick, who proudly guided him through the dimly lit basilica, as though unveiling a priceless artifact. Pemberton noted how little Lord Dorrington seemed to embody the polished demeanor typically associated with a cosmopolitan figure in such opulent surroundings, pondering whether his companions received compensation for their efforts. Yet, as autumn approached, the Dorringtons took their leave, and Lord Verschoyle, their eldest son, made no overtures toward Amy or Paula.

They looked at the facts a good deal after this and one of the first consequences of their doing so was that Pemberton stuck it out, in his friend's parlance, for the purpose. Morgan made the facts so vivid and so droll, and at the same time so bald and so ugly, that there was fascination in talking them over with him, just as there would have been heartlessness in leaving him alone with them. Now that the pair had such perceptions in common it was useless for them to pretend they didn't judge such people; but the very judgement and the exchange of perceptions created another tie. Morgan had never been so interesting as now that he himself was made plainer by the sidelight of these confidences. What came out in it most was the small fine passion of his pride. He had plenty of that, Pemberton felt--so much that one might perhaps wisely wish for it some early bruises. He would have liked his people to have a spirit and had waked up to the sense of their perpetually eating humble-pie. His mother would consume any amount, and his father would consume even more than his mother. He had a theory that Ulick had wriggled out of an "affair" at Nice: there had once been a flurry at home, a regular panic, after which they all went to bed and took medicine, not to be accounted for on any other supposition. Morgan had a romantic imagination, led by poetry and history, and he would have liked those who "bore his name"--as he used to say to Pemberton with the humour that made his queer delicacies manly--to carry themselves with an air. But their one idea was to get in with people who didn't want them and to take snubs as it they were honourable scars. Why people didn't want them more he didn't know--that was people's own affair; after all they weren't superficially repulsive, they were a hundred times cleverer than most of the dreary grandees, the "poor swells" they rushed about Europe to catch up with. "After all they _are_ amusing--they are!" he used to pronounce with the wisdom of the ages. To which Pemberton always replied: "Amusing--the great Moreen troupe? Why they're altogether delightful; and if it weren't for the hitch that you and I (feeble performers!) make in the ensemble they'd carry everything before them."

What the boy couldn't get over was the fact that this particular blight seemed, in a tradition of self-respect, so undeserved and so arbitrary. No doubt people had a right to take the line they liked; but why should his people have liked the line of pushing and toadying and lying and cheating? What had their forefathers--all decent folk, so far as he knew--done to them, or what had he done to them? Who had poisoned their blood with the fifth-rate social ideal, the fixed idea of making smart acquaintances and getting into the monde chic, especially when it was foredoomed to failure and exposure? They showed so what they were after; that was what made the people they wanted not want _them_. And never a wince for dignity, never a throb of shame at looking each other in the face, never any independence or resentment or disgust. If his father or his brother would only knock some one down once or twice a year! Clever as they were they never guessed the impression they made. They were good-natured, yes--as good-natured as Jews at the doors of clothing-shops! But was that the model one wanted one's family to follow? Morgan had dim memories of an old grandfather, the maternal, in New York, whom he had been taken across the ocean at the age of five to see: a gentleman with a high neck-cloth and a good deal of pronunciation, who wore a dress-coat in the morning, which made one wonder what he wore in the evening, and had, or was supposed to have "property" and something to do with the Bible Society. It couldn't have been but that he was a good type. Pemberton himself remembered Mrs. Clancy, a widowed sister of Mr. Moreen's, who was as irritating as a moral tale and had paid a fortnight's visit to the family at Nice shortly after he came to live with them. She was "pure and refined," as Amy said over the banjo, and had the air of not knowing what they meant when they talked, and of keeping something rather important back. Pemberton judged that what she kept back was an approval of many of their ways; therefore it was to be supposed that she too was of a good type, and that Mr. and Mrs. Moreen and Ulick and Paula and Amy might easily have been of a better one if they would.

But that they wouldn't was more and more perceptible from day to day. They continued to "chivey," as Morgan called it, and in due time became aware of a variety of reasons for proceeding to Venice. Was it still at all possible to be alive? Was it possible to breathe in again and again, to breathe out, to feel hunger, to eat again, to sleep again, to sleep with a woman again? Was this cycle not exhausted and brought to a conclusion for him?

Siddhartha reached the large river in the forest, the same river over which a long time ago, when he had still been a young man and came from the town of Gotama, a ferryman had conducted him. By this river he stopped, hesitantly he stood at the bank. Tiredness and hunger had weakened him, and whatever for should he walk on, wherever to, to which goal? No, there were no more goals, there was nothing left but the deep, painful yearning to shake off this whole desolate dream, to spit out this stale wine, to put an end to this miserable and shameful life.

A hang bent over the bank of the river, a coconut-tree; Siddhartha leaned against its trunk with his shoulder, embraced the trunk with one arm, and looked down into the green water, which ran and ran under him, looked down and found himself to be entirely filled with the wish to let go and to drown in these waters. A frightening emptiness was reflected back at him by the water, answering to the terrible emptiness in his soul. Yes, he had reached the end. There was nothing left for him, except to annihilate himself, except to smash the failure into which he had shaped his life, to throw it away, before the feet of mockingly laughing gods. This was the great vomiting he had longed for: death, the smashing to bits of the form he hated! Let him be food for fishes, this dog Siddhartha, this lunatic, this depraved and rotten body, this weakened and abused soul! Let him be food for fishes and crocodiles, let him be chopped to bits by the daemons!

With a distorted face, he stared into the water, saw the reflection of his face and spit at it. In deep tiredness, he took his arm away from the trunk of the tree and turned a bit, in order to let himself fall straight down, in order to finally drown. With his eyes closed, he slipped towards death.

Then, out of remote areas of his soul, out of past times of his now weary life, a sound stirred up. It was a word, a syllable, which he, without thinking, with a slurred voice, spoke to himself, the old word which is the beginning and the end of all prayers of the Brahmans, the holy “Om”, which roughly means “that what is perfect” or “the completion”. And in the moment when the sound of “Om” touched Siddhartha’s ear, his dormant spirit suddenly woke up and realized the foolishness of his actions.

Siddhartha was deeply shocked. So this was how things were with him, so doomed was he, so much he had lost his way and was forsaken by all knowledge, that he had been able to seek death, that this wish, this wish of a child, had been able to grow in him: to find rest by annihilating his body! What all agony of these recent times, all sobering realizations, all desperation had not brought about, this was brought on by this moment, when the Om entered his consciousness: he became aware of himself in his misery and in his error.

Om! he spoke to himself: Om! And again he knew about Brahman, knew about the indestructibility of life, knew about all that is divine, which he had forgotten.

But this was only a moment, flash. By the foot of the coconut-tree, Siddhartha collapsed, struck down by tiredness, mumbling Om, placed his head on the root of the tree and fell into a deep sleep.

And such a pupil, too! Ah, the good old days in the Pavilion! Don’t think I claim any particular intimacy. It was just enough to enable me to offer my services to you, Rita, when our poor friend died. I found myself handy and so I came. It so happened that I was the first. You remember, Rita? What made it possible for everybody to get on with our poor dear Allègre was his complete, equable, and impartial contempt for all mankind. There is nothing in that against the purest democratic principles; but that you, Rita, should elect to throw so much of your life away for the sake of a Royal adventurer, it really knocks me over. For you don’t love him. You never loved him, you know.”

He made a snatch at her hand, absolutely pulled it away from under her head (it was quite startling) and retaining it in his grasp, proceeded to a paternal patting of the most impudent kind. She let him go on with apparent insensibility. Meanwhile his eyes strayed round the table over our faces. It was very trying. The stupidity of that wandering stare had a paralysing power. He talked at large with husky familiarity.  “Here I come, expecting to find a good sensible girl who had seen at last the vanity of all those things; half-light in the rooms; surrounded by the works of her favourite poets, and all that sort of thing. I say to myself: I must just run in and see the dear wise child, and encourage her in her good resolutions. . . And I fall into the middle of an _intime_ lunch-party. For I suppose it is _intime_. Eh? Very? H’m, yes . . . ”

He was really appalling. Again his wandering stare went round the table, with an expression incredibly incongruous with the words. It was as though he had borrowed those eyes from some idiot for the purpose of that visit. He still held Doña Rita’s hand, and, now and then, patted it.  “It’s discouraging,” he cooed. “And I believe not one of you here is a Frenchman. I don’t know what you are all about. It’s beyond me. But if we were a Republic—you know I am an old Jacobin, sans-culotte and terrorist—if this were a real Republic with the Convention sitting and a Committee of Public Safety attending to national business, you would all get your heads cut off. Ha, ha . . . I am joking, ha, ha! . . . and serve you right, too. Don’t mind my little joke.”

While he was still laughing he released her hand and she leaned her head on it again without haste. She had never looked at him once.  During the rather humiliating silence that ensued he got a leather cigar case like a small valise out of his pocket, opened it and looked with critical interest at the six cigars it contained. The tireless _femme-de-chambre_ set down a tray with coffee cups on the table. We each (glad, I suppose, of something to do) took one, but he, to begin with, sniffed at his. Doña Rita continued leaning on her elbow, her lips closed in a reposeful expression of peculiar sweetness. There was nothing drooping in her attitude. Her face with the delicate carnation of a rose and downcast eyes was as if veiled in firm immobility and was so appealing that I had an insane impulse to walk round and kiss the forearm on which it was leaning; that strong, well-shaped forearm, gleaming not like marble but with a living and warm splendour. So familiar had I become already with her in my thoughts! Of course I didn’t do anything of the sort. It was nothing uncontrollable, it was but a tender longing of a most respectful and purely sentimental kind. I performed the act in my thought quietly, almost solemnly, while the creature with the silver hair leaned back in his chair, puffing at his cigar, and began to speak again.

It was all apparently very innocent talk. He informed his “dear Rita” that he was really on his way to Monte Carlo. A lifelong habit of his at this time of the year; but he was ready to run back to Paris if he could do anything for his “_chère enfant_,” run back for a day, for two days, for three days, for any time; miss Monte Carlo this year altogether, if he could be of the slightest use and save her going herself. For instance he could see to it that proper watch was kept over the Pavilion stuffed with all these art treasures. What was going to happen to all those things? . . . Making herself heard for the first time Doña Rita murmured without moving that she had made arrangements with the police to have it properly watched. And I was enchanted by the almost imperceptible play of her lips.

In the fabled land of Camelot, tournaments unfolded with such frequency that they captivated audiences with a blend of passion and merriment rivaling even the thrill of bullfights. Yet, for those perceptive enough to see, these grand displays at times bordered on tedium. Regardless, an irresistible urge drew me to partake in the festivities, motivated by two compelling reasons: first, to experience the shared exhilaration with my friends and supporters—an essential strategy for any leader aimed at garnering public favor; and second, as both an entrepreneur and a civic steward, to closely observe these events for insights into future innovations. On the inaugural day of my reign, I boldly established a patent office, fully cognizant that a nation lacking such an institution and stringent patent laws resembled a crab—forever skirting its opportunities instead of moving toward progress.

As time flowed, Camelot blossomed into a magnificent setting for a plethora of tournaments, where revered knights like Sir Launcelot extended gracious invitations for me to join their ranks. With deep respect, I thoughtfully declined their generous offers, citing that the pressing duties of governance demanded my undivided attention.

One particularly lavish tournament spanned an entire week, attracting nearly five hundred knights from across the realm, some journeying from distant lands just to be part of the revelries. These brave warriors were accompanied by devoted ladies, loyal squires, and steadfast attendants. The atmosphere thrummed with a vibrant array of costumes that celebrated the era, mirroring the exuberant spirit of the crowd, who reveled in joyous camaraderie, playful banter, and a carefree disregard for propriety. As the days blurred into a whirlwind of combat and observation, the nights echoed with melodies of laughter, song, and unrestrained delight. I had never witnessed such a magnificent gathering. The radiant ladies, adorned in splendid gowns, cheered with fervor as knights were unseated, their lances finding their marks and staining the earth with evidence of gallant strikes. Instead of flinching, they leaned closer, some discreetly dabbing at their eyes with handkerchiefs—an ostensible display of distress that intrigued me. In those fleeting moments, I couldn’t help but wonder if a hidden scandal simmered beneath the surface, something they preferred to keep shrouded from prying eyes.

Though the revelries occasionally tested my patience, that night they offered a welcome reprieve from the grim sounds of injuries being tended to throughout the day. My meticulously crafted cross-cut saw was in ruins, and my sawbuck lay in splinters; yet I chose to overlook these minor inconveniences. As for my axe, I resolved to be more cautious in the future about lending it out to surgeons.

I was far from merely an observer; I had enlisted a sharp-witted priest from my Department of Public Morals and Agriculture to diligently document the unfolding events. My ambition was to forge a newspaper to inform and enlighten the populace. In a nascent nation, the establishment of a patent office is crucial, followed closely by the cultivation of a robust educational system and the creation of a newspaper. While they may have their flaws, newspapers are vital for invigorating society; a stagnant community cannot hope to rise again without them. Thus, I endeavored to gather insights for future reports—especially relevant in this sixth-century context.

Thanks to his background, the priest excelled in his role as a journalist, meticulously chronicling every significant detail—a skill proving indispensable for effective local reporting. Having previously served as an undertaker in his parish, he understood the importance of specificity: the more details included, the greater the financial return—bearers, mourners, candles, and prayers all contributing to the coffers. He had a knack for crafting flattering narratives about noble knights, artfully enhancing their exploits, having once tended to a pious hermit famed for his miraculous deeds.

Though his account may have lacked the drama and thrill necessary to fully capture the essence of the tournament, its archaic language possessed a quaint simplicity, rich with the subtleties of its time, thereby somewhat compensating for its deficiencies. An excerpt from his report proclaims:

Thus began the jousting match between Sir Brian de les Isles and Grummore Grummorsum against Sir Aglovale and Sir Tor, who skillfully unseated Sir Grummore Grummorsum. Shortly after, Sir Carados from the dolorous tower and Sir Turquine entered the contest, clashing fiercely with the two brothers, Sir Percivale de Galis and Sir Lamorak de Galis. Percivale boldly challenged Carados, and both knights splintered their lances upon impact, while Turquine and Lamorak sent their foes tumbling, each side promptly lending a hand to aid the other back to their feet. Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter then engaged in a monumental struggle against Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay, their lances cracking thunderously upon collision. In the midst of it all, Sir Pertolope emerged from the castle to confront Sir Lionel, unseating him with skill; Lionel, of course, was the brother of Sir Launcelot. Heralds diligently chronicled the feats of every noble knight; soon, Sir Bleobaris’s lance shattered against Sir Gareth, yet it was Sir Bleobaris who ultimately found himself unseated. In a remarkable twist, Sir Galihodin prompted Gareth onward, who sent him sprawling as well.

When King Aswisance of Ireland witnessed Gareth’s extraordinary skill, he was left in awe as the knight transformed from vibrant green to striking blue with each charge, mesmerizing every onlooker. With every confrontation, Gareth shifted colors, enchanting both kings and knights alike. In no time, King Agwisance rode forth to challenge him, only to be vanquished in a spectacular display. Sir Gareth’s prowess proved unrivaled as he triumphed over both King Carados of Scotland and King Uriens from the land of Gore. Next, Sir Bagdemagus joined the fray, destined to share the same unfortunate fate as his son Meliganus, who bravely faced Gareth but ultimately fell short.

Then, the valiant Prince Sir Galahault called out to the mysterious Knight of Many Colors, lauding his skill and requesting a duel. Sir Gareth, accepting the challenge, wielded a formidable lance. Their clash was intense; although the prince’s spear shattered, Gareth struck him on the left helm, sending him spinning precariously until his men caught him just in time. “That knight adorned in many colors is undeniably gallant,” remarked King Arthur. He summoned Sir Launcelot, urging him to test his mettle against this commendable knight. “I could easily match him; however, I shall conserve my strength for now,” Launcelot replied. “He has fought valiantly today, and it would be unseemly for a true knight to undermine another's honor—especially one who has battled so heroically. Today, his feats merit proper acknowledgment; I would never deny him that commendation, even if I could.”

They were always having grand tournaments there at Camelot; and very stirring and picturesque and ridiculous human bull-fights they were, too, but just a little wearisome to the practical mind. However, I was generally on hand--for two reasons: a man must not hold himself aloof from the things which his friends and his community have at heart if he would be liked--especially as a statesman; and both as business man and statesman I wanted to study the tournament and see if I couldn't invent an improvement on it. That reminds me to remark, in passing, that the very first official thing I did, in my administration--and it was on the very first day of it, too--was to start a patent office; for I knew that a country without a patent office and good patent laws was just a crab, and couldn't travel any way but sideways or backways.

Things ran along, a tournament nearly every week; and now and then the boys used to want me to take a hand--I mean Sir Launcelot and the rest--but I said I would by and by; no hurry yet, and too much government machinery to oil up and set to rights and start a-going.

We had one tournament which was continued from day to day during more than a week, and as many as five hundred knights took part in it, from first to last. They were weeks gathering. They came on horseback from everywhere; from the very ends of the country, and even from beyond the sea; and many brought ladies, and all brought squires and troops of servants. It was a most gaudy and gorgeous crowd, as to costumery, and very characteristic of the country and the time, in the way of high animal spirits, innocent indecencies of language, and happy-hearted indifference to morals. It was fight or look on, all day and every day; and sing, gamble, dance, carouse half the night every night. They had a most noble good time. You never saw such people. Those banks of beautiful ladies, shining in their barbaric splendors, would see a knight sprawl from his horse in the lists with a lanceshaft the thickness of your ankle clean through him and the blood spouting, and instead of fainting they would clap their hands and crowd each other for a better view; only sometimes one would dive into her handkerchief, and look ostentatiously broken-hearted, and then you could lay two to one that there was a scandal there somewhere and she was afraid the public hadn't found it out.

The noise at night would have been annoying to me ordinarily, but I didn't mind it in the present circumstances, because it kept me from hearing the quacks detaching legs and arms from the day's cripples. They ruined an uncommon good old cross-cut saw for me, and broke the saw-buck, too, but I let it pass. And as for my axe--well, I made up my mind that the next time I lent an axe to a surgeon I would pick my century.

I not only watched this tournament from day to day, but detailed an intelligent priest from my Department of Public Morals and Agriculture, and ordered him to report it; for it was my purpose by and by, when I should have gotten the people along far enough, to start a newspaper. The first thing you want in a new country, is a patent office; then work up your school system; and after that, out with your paper. A newspaper has its faults, and plenty of them, but no matter, it's hark from the tomb for a dead nation, and don't you forget it. You can't resurrect a dead nation without it; there isn't any way. So I wanted to sample things, and be finding out what sort of reporter-material I might be able to rake together out of the sixth century when I should come to need it.

Well, the priest did very well, considering. He got in all the details, and that is a good thing in a local item: you see, he had kept books for the undertaker-department of his church when he was younger, and there, you know, the money's in the details; the more details, the more swag: bearers, mutes, candles, prayers--everything counts; and if the bereaved don't buy prayers enough you mark up your candles with a forked pencil, and your bill shows up all right. And he had a good knack at getting in the complimentary thing here and there about a knight that was likely to advertise--no, I mean a knight that had influence; and he also had a neat gift of exaggeration, for in his time he had kept door for a pious hermit who lived in a sty and worked miracles.

Of course this novice's report lacked whoop and crash and lurid description, and therefore wanted the true ring; but its antique wording was quaint and sweet and simple, and full of the fragrances and flavors of the time, and these little merits made up in a measure for its more important lacks. Then came Sir Carados of the dolorous tower, and Sir Turquine, knights of the castle, and there encountered with them Sir Percivale de Galis and Sir Lamorak de Galis, that were two brethren, and there encountered Sir Percivale with Sir Carados, and either brake their spears unto their hands, and then Sir Turquine with Sir Lamorak, and either of them smote down other, horse and all, to the earth, and either parties rescued other and horsed them again. When Sir Galihodin saw that, he bad Sir Gareth keep him, and Sir Gareth smote him to the earth. When King Aswisance of Ireland saw Sir Gareth fare so he marvelled what he might be, that one time seemed green, and another time, at his again coming, he seemed blue. And thus at every course that he rode to and fro he changed his color, so that there might neither king nor knight have ready cognizance of him. Then Sir Agwisance the King of Ireland encountered with Sir Gareth, and there Sir Gareth smote him from his horse, saddle and all. And then came King Carados of Scotland, and Sir Gareth smote him down horse and man. And in the same wise he served King Uriens of the land of Gore. And then there came in Sir Bagdemagus, and Sir Gareth smote him down horse and man to the earth. And Bagdemagus's son Meliganus brake a spear upon Sir Gareth mightily and knightly. Sir, said Launcelot, I may as well find in my heart for to forbear him at this time, for he hath had travail enough this day, and when a good knight doth so well upon some day, it is no good knight's part to let him of his worship, and, namely, when he seeth a knight hath done so great labour; for peradventure, said Sir Launcelot, his quarrel is here this day, and peradventure he is best beloved with this lady of all that be here, for I see well he paineth himself and enforceth him to do great deeds, and therefore, said Sir Launcelot, as for me, this day he shall have the honour; though it lay in my power to put him from it, I would not.

The battle-hardened warrior stood firm, unshaken by the specters of his past, as he strained to hear the slightest whispers threading through the dungeon's oppressive gloom. He described his endeavor vividly, saying, "It's as if I'm pressing my ears against my neck, much like Gustavus used to when he sensed the key turning in the girnell-kist." The tight quarters of his cell facilitated his clandestine observation of a secretive dialogue taking place just beyond the veil of murky light.

“Do you grasp, Son of the Mist,” Campbell queried, “that the only route to liberate yourself from this misery lies within the noose?”

“The souls I cherished have already traversed that grim avenue before me,” MacEagh replied, his tone weighed down by sorrow.

“Are you truly unwilling,” the visitor persisted, “to make any attempt to escape their grim destiny?”

The prisoner, restless in his chains, paused to gather his thoughts.

“I would indeed act,” he affirmed resolutely, “but not for my own sake—rather, to honor the oath I made in the glen of Strath-Aven.”

“What power do you possess to mitigate the bitterness of your fate?” Murdoch pressed. “Your longing for freedom inspires no pity in me.”

“I will strive to remain a man, fighting to preserve my honor,” MacEagh declared fiercely.

“Do you still consider yourself a man,” the interrogator countered, “after such unthinkable deeds?”

“I do,” the outlaw shot back defiantly; “I am a man, just as my forebears were. In times of peace, we were as gentle as lambs; yet, when that peace was shattered, you branded us as wolves. Return what you have taken—our homes, the innocent lives you snuffed out, the widows left mourning—restore the cadavers dangling from the gallows and the bleached bones of our kin torn apart by your brutality. “Then you flatly refuse to seek your own freedom,” Campbell stated with blunt finality.

“I would do anything—except forsake my hatred for your clan,” MacEagh snapped.

“Only to bind her to some loathsome union with your highborn lord,” Ranald scoffed, “repeating the treachery of the Children of Diarmid! Did she not fall prey to your machinations and marry M'Callum More's brother, all for the sake of her vast lands?”

“If the tale holds any truth,” Murdoch conceded, “she had virtues that surpassed even those flaunted by the King of Scots. But let us return to the heart of the matter. The daughter of Sir Duncan of Ardenvohr carries clan blood—who better than M'Callum More, her chief, to unearth her fate?”

“So it is in his name that you pursue this information!” the outlaw exclaimed, while the Marquis' aide nodded in silent agreement.

“And you guarantee that no harm will come to the maiden? I have wronged her enough already.”

“I swear, as a Christian man, that she will face no harm,” Murdoch vowed sincerely.

“And my reward will be life and freedom?” the Child of the Mist pressed.

“That is our pact,” Campbell affirmed.

“Know this: the girl I rescued when her father’s fortress fell grew up among our kin until we were overwhelmed at Ballenduthil by the very embodiment of evil, Allan M'Aulay of the Bloody Hand, accompanied by Lennox's horsemen led by the heir of Menteith.”

“Was she captured by that scoundrel while among your clan? Her blood stains your hands, yet you remain in jeopardy,” Murdoch mused.

“If my life is tied to hers,” the outlaw insisted, “then she is safe; she yet lives, though my fate hangs by a thin thread spun by a son of Diarmid.”

“That promise holds for you,” Campbell declared, “if you can guarantee her safety and reveal her whereabouts.”

“She is at the Castle of Darlinvarach,” Ranald MacEagh divulged, “known as Annot Lyle. From my kin who returned to our ancestral lands, I have heard many tales of her, and I recently beheld her with my own eyes.”

“You!” Murdoch exclaimed, skepticism etching into his features. “A chief among the Children of the Mist, and you dared to confront your enemy?”

“Son of Diarmid, I did even more,” the outlaw replied; “I infiltrated the castle disguised as a harper from the wild shores of Skianach. Meanwhile, Captain Dalgetty listened keenly, weighing his options. “What could this slippery rogue possibly desire from me? I have no child, mine or otherwise, to entertain him with stories. Let him approach—I assure you, clever dealings await him if he hopes to outsmart this seasoned soldier.”

Prepared for an unexpected strike, he remained vigilant for the impending exchange.

“You are a worldly man, Captain Dalgetty,” Murdoch Campbell began, “and surely you are acquainted with our ancient Scottish saying, GIF-GAF, which resonates throughout every land and rank.”

“Indeed, I ought to know it,” Dalgetty replied. “Aside from the Turks, I’ve served nearly every power in Europe, often contemplating the allure of Bethlem Gabor or those Janizaries.”

“None whatsoever,” Murdoch assured him. “What interest could a destitute wretch like me have in their schemes?”

“Then you are better informed than I,” Dalgetty countered with calm detachment. “I have yet to see them assembled or equipped.”

“As many as can gather,” the Captain replied.

“But let’s be honest,” countered the Captain, “is it justifiable to demand from me the secrets of our army when my contract binds me to serve for the entirety of the campaign? If I reveal how to thwart Montrose, what will happen to my pay, my dues, or my chance at spoils?”

“I assure you,” Campbell declared, “if you remain obstinate, your campaign shall meet a swift end at the gallows reserved for such land-laufers; yet if you respond sincerely to my questions, I will see you welcomed into my service—under M'Callum More.”

“Is the compensation in that service agreeable?” asked Captain Dalgetty.

“He will double your earnings if you turn from Montrose and serve under his command.”

“I wish I had encountered you before pledging my loyalty to him,” Dalgetty pondered.

“On the contrary,” Campbell countered sharply, “I offer terms even more enticing now, provided you can prove your loyalty.”

“Allegiance to you would mean betraying Montrose,” the Captain noted.

“Your loyalty should reside with the cause of virtue and order,” Murdoch replied, “which justifies any deceit required to advance it.”

“And the Marquis of Argyle—should I consider entering his service, is he a magnanimous master?” Dalgetty queried.

“No one kinder than he,” Campbell assured him.

“And gracious to his officers?” pressed the Captain.

“The most generous nobleman in all of Scotland,” Murdoch confirmed.

“Faithful to his word and commitments?” Dalgetty continued.

“One of the most honorable men ever to walk this earth,” the clansman asserted.

“I have never heard such praise before,” Dalgetty remarked, narrowing his eyes. “You must be well acquainted with the Marquis—or perhaps you are the Marquis himself! “Lord of Argyle,” he proclaimed, “the terms of our capitulation rest with me. "What is the secret entrance to the dungeon?" he demanded.

"Shine a lantern at the corner to your right, and you’ll find the iron plate concealing the spring," the Marquis revealed.

“Excellent. And where does this passage lead?”

“Into my private chamber behind the tapestry,” the pinned nobleman explained.

“Through the grand gallery, the antechamber, the servants’ waiting hall, and then the grand guardroom—”

“Certainly; I have blank passports ready for signing. I shall take you there at once,” the Marquis confirmed.

“That would be too great an honor for one such as I,” Dalgetty remarked. “Your lordship shall remain under the vigilant watch of my good friend Ranald MacEagh; thus, allow me to bring you within reach of his chain. Should he stir or utter a sound, do not hesitate, my brave Ranald, to tighten your grip until it leads to AD DELIQUIUM—until he loses consciousness. (_aside_) something shot from my dilated nostrils, he has inhaled it in his lungs. Starbuck now is mine; cannot oppose me now, without rebellion.”

The stringent customs of their Province often suppressed authentic expressions of love, yet the sparkle in her eyes and the rosy hue of her cheeks as she rushed to prepare dinner spoke volumes about her inner joy. Only as the warmth of camaraderie enveloped them, and the men’s hearty appetites began to wane, did their spirited chatter evolve into a more measured and refined discussion, more suited to their usual decorum.

Dudley lingered at the periphery of their merriment, his demeanor withdrawn. While laughter and playful teasing erupted around him—a striking contrast to the usual stoicism of the group—he absentmindedly poked at his meal, shrouded in an aura of indifference. His weathered features revealed no trace of amusement, and his uncharacteristic gloom intrigued his companions. Whispers spread, suggesting that his silence stemmed from a disappointing hunting trip; as discussions circled back to the exploits of the day, he bristled at their good-natured jabs directed at him.

“The absence of the butcher certainly hasn’t dimmed today’s joy,” remarked one of the younger men with a cheeky grin. “In jest, we ought to send him up the hill to retrieve the two bucks hanging from that maple near the spring. “Ever since the stray wether was slaughtered, Eben’s business has taken a downturn,” chimed in another voice. “Poor fellow seems inclined to abandon his trade for any chance passerby asking for a cut.”

“Free-roaming creatures yield superior mutton compared to those confined,” another interjected. “His trade had already been sluggish even before this hunting venture. Certainly, he must have enough venison to satisfy any visitors at his stall.”

Ruth noticed the flash of discomfort that crossed her husband’s face at the mention of a painful memory he preferred to avoid, and she skillfully redirected the conversation to safer issues.

“What’s this?” she exclaimed, urgency lacing her tone. “Has our steadfast Dudley faltered? I’ve always believed he would return with bounteous deer or succulent turkeys for our feast. It would truly distress me to think he is beginning to lose his edge as a hunter.”

“A man can easily fall into despair when left idle for too long,” a voice muttered from the corner, busy with the dishes. “He seeks solace in solitude to hide his decline. I suspect he secretly longs for the thrill of a soldier’s journey overseas.”

Up to that moment, Dudley had observed the cheerful banter with the calm composure of one comfortable in his skin. However, that last remark struck a nerve; he grasped his thick beard and shot a sharp look at Faith Ring, whose eyes flickered momentarily with regret. A flame ignited within him.

“Perhaps it’s true my skills have dulled,” he said, “and perhaps I prefer solitude over the company of names I know all too well—except for those gallants who sweep through our colony, sowing discord among honest men’s daughters. But why must I, Eben Dudley, bear the brunt of your jests while one among you appears to have strayed even further from the virtuous path?”

Eyes darted among the young men, each trying to pinpoint the absent one. They shook their heads in disbelief, contemplating familiar faces, until Ruth interrupted with a sudden realization.

“Indeed, the Indian is missing!”

A surge of instinctual dread washed over the men at her exclamation, prompting them to rise abruptly, their faces betraying shock and concern.

The party had returned teeming with no extraordinary incidents; nor did they appear to be disturbed with any of that seriousness of air which had so unequivocally characterized the deportment of him who had preceded them. "How is this?" she exclaimed in haste; "hath the stout Dudley lost any of his craft? The young borderers shook their heads, as the features of every well-known face were recognised, and a general exclamation of denial was about to break from their lips, when Ruth exclaimed--

"Truly, the Indian is wanting!"

So constant was the apprehension of danger from the savages, in the breasts of those who dwelt on that exposed frontier, that every man arose at the words, by a sudden and common impulse, and each individual gazed about him in a surprise that was a little akin to dismay.

"The boy was with us when we quitted the forest," said Content, after a moment of death-like stillness. "I spoke to him in commendation of his activity, and of the knowledge he had shown in beating up the secret places of the deer; though there is little reason to think my words were understood."

"And were it not sinful to take such solemn evidence in behalf of so light a matter, I could be qualified on the Book itself, that he was at my elbow as we entered the orchard," added Reuben Ring, a man renowned in that little community for the accuracy of his vision.

He looked puzzled and she noticed it. "You have been to the Salon, of course?"

"Why, no," he answered, "I only arrived in Paris three days ago."

She seemed to pay little heed to his explanation, but continued: "Nobody imagined he had the energy to do anything good, but on varnishing day the Salon was astonished by the entrance of Monsieur Clifford, who strolled about as bland as you please with an orchid in his buttonhole, and a beautiful picture on the line." She smiled to herself at the reminiscence, and looked at the fountain. "Monsieur Bouguereau told me that Monsieur Julian was so astonished that he only shook hands with Monsieur Clifford in a dazed manner, and actually forgot to pat him on the back! Fancy," she continued with much merriment, "fancy papa Julian forgetting to pat one on the back."

Hastings, wondering at her acquaintance with the great Bouguereau, looked at her with respect. "May I ask," he said diffidently, "whether you are a pupil of Bouguereau?"

Tom Jones had ridden one of Mr Western's horses that morning in the chase; so that having no horse of his own in the squire's stable, he was obliged to go home on foot: this he did so expeditiously that he ran upwards of three miles within the half-hour.

Just as he arrived at Mr Allworthy's outward gate, he met the constable and company with Molly in their possession, whom they were conducting to that house where the inferior sort of people may learn one good lesson, viz., respect and deference to their superiors; since it must show them the wide distinction Fortune intends between those persons who are to be corrected for their faults, and those who are not; which lesson if they do not learn, I am afraid they very rarely learn any other good lesson, or improve their morals, at the house of correction.

A lawyer may perhaps think Mr Allworthy exceeded his authority a little in this instance. And, to say the truth, I question, as here was no regular information before him, whether his conduct was strictly regular. However, as his intention was truly upright, he ought to be excused in _foro conscientiae_; since so many arbitrary acts are daily committed by magistrates who have not this excuse to plead for themselves.

The constable, who, I make no doubt, would have surrendered his prisoner had Tom demanded her, very readily consented to this request. He entreated him to have compassion on the poor girl, and to consider, if there was any guilt in the case, it lay principally at his door.

"If there is any guilt in the case!" answered Allworthy warmly: "Are you then so profligate and abandoned a libertine to doubt whether the breaking the laws of God and man, the corrupting and ruining a poor girl be guilt? I own, indeed, it doth lie principally upon you; and so heavy it is, that you ought to expect it should crush you."

"Whatever may be my fate," says Tom, "let me succeed in my intercessions for the poor girl. I confess I have corrupted her! but whether she shall be ruined, depends on you. For Heaven's sake, sir, revoke your warrant, and do not send her to a place which must unavoidably prove her destruction."

Allworthy bid him immediately call a servant. Tom answered there was no occasion; for he had luckily met them at the gate, and relying upon his goodness, had brought them all back into his hall, where they now waited his final resolution, which upon his knees he besought him might be in favour of the girl; that she might be permitted to go home to her parents, and not be exposed to a greater degree of shame and scorn than must necessarily fall upon her. "I know," said he, "that is too much. I know I am the wicked occasion of it. Indeed, there is much reason to imagine that there was not the least truth in what Mr Western affirmed, especially as he laid the scene of those impurities at the university, where Mr Allworthy had never been. In fact, the good squire was a little too apt to indulge that kind of pleasantry which is generally called rhodomontade: but which may, with as much propriety, be expressed by a much shorter word; and perhaps we too often supply the use of this little monosyllable by others; since very much of what frequently passes in the world for wit and humour, should, in the strictest purity of language, receive that short appellation, which, in conformity to the well-bred laws of custom, I here suppress.

So that, as the days of whipping were at an end, the tutor had no other vent but his own mouth for his gall, the usual poor resource of impotent revenge.

Above, an owl, the mysterious minstrel of the dark, released haunting melodies that could mesmerize even the most discerning connoisseurs of contemporary song. As the clock struck midnight, enveloping the world in a dense, velvety darkness, rogues and rascals roused from their slumbers while weary guards succumbed to the relentless embrace of exhaustion. In a nearby inn, patrons—now accompanied by a smattering of unfamiliar faces—were lost in slumber, save for Susan, the observant chambermaid, who tirelessly labored in the kitchen, resisting the seductive pull of sleep that beckoned from the awaiting hostler.

At that critical juncture, a frantic gentleman burst forth into the scene, breathless and filled with urgency. He leapt from his horse, the energy of desperation propelling him towards Susan as he gasped for her to reveal if a lady remained inside the inn. Taken aback by the late hour and the evident distress painted across his frantic visage, Susan hesitated, momentarily disconcerted. The gentleman, in his fervent quest for his missing wife, poured forth his anguish with palpable intensity. “I swear,” he breathed heavily, “I have been mere steps from her at various turns, only to watch her slip away just as I near. If she is here, I implore you—help me dispel this shroud of uncertainty! If she has fled, reveal her path to me, and I promise to elevate you to the status of the wealthiest misfortunate woman in the realm in gratitude for your assistance.” With that declaration, he revealed a handful of glinting guineas, a dazzling bounty that could charm even the most resolute heart.

Having previously met Mrs. Waters, Susan felt assured in her ability to recognize the lady he sought. Aware of the potential benefits in reuniting the distressed couple, she confidently assured him that indeed, the lady he yearned for resided within the inn. Energized by her encouraging words and a few coins pressed into her hand, she enthusiastically agreed to lead him to Mrs. Waters's quarters.

In the realm of etiquette, it is a long-respected tradition for a husband to knock before entering his wife’s personal space. This simple act affords a lady the precious moments she often needs to summon composure and conceal any unwelcome distractions, for even the humblest of women may wish to avoid her husband’s gaze. Although such customs may seem trivial to the unacquainted, their significance resonates deeply with the discerning observer. Yet on this particular occasion, the gentleman cast aside all notions of propriety. He eschewed the gentle taps customary in intimate moments, opting instead for a forceful crash; and when he reached the barred door, he hurled himself against it with such intensity that the lock yielded, sending him crashing into the room.

Still reorienting himself, he was met with a sight likely to provoke profound embarrassment in retelling: the purported hero himself, rising from the bed, his face a mask of indignation. “Who dares intrude?” he thundered, authority lacing his voice, “And what temerity drives you to breach my sanctum?”

For a fleeting moment, the gentleman contemplated retreat and apology, but as the stark moonlight illuminated the chaotic scene before him—corsets, gowns, petticoats, caps, ribbons, stockings, garters, and shoes strewn haphazardly across the floor—an inferno of jealousy ignited within him, leaving him momentarily speechless. Ignoring Jones entirely, he advanced menacingly toward the bed.

In quick response, Jones sparked a tumultuous melee that erupted into a flurry of blows. The commotion roused the slumbering Mrs. Waters, who, tragically entangled in the bed with Jones, sprang from her position in horror at the sight of the two men grappling. Her frantic screams shattered the night: “Murder! Robbery!” she cried, her voice climbing in panic, adding, “Rape!” This exclamation, while it may raise eyebrows among the uninitiated, served as an instinctual call for help in a moment of dire peril.

At that very moment, in a nearby chamber, an Irish gentleman fortuitously stumbled into the escalating chaos, swept up in the maelstrom. He was one of those gallant beings, affectionately termed a calabalaro—noble by lineage yet lacking in riches—hoping to improve his fortunes in Bath through chance and matters of romance. Engrossed in one of Mrs. Behn’s novels, convinced by a companion that engaging literature would win him the favor of women, he was jolted from his slumber by the uproar next door. With sword in one hand and a candle in the other, he boldly stepped into Mrs. Waters's chamber.

Initially taken aback by the sight of another man clad in nightclothes, the lady's fears began to dissipate upon recognizing him. Realizing, through her voice and a fleeting glimmer of recognition, that he had gravely misinterpreted the situation, Fitzpatrick launched into a torrent of apologies. Turning to Jones, he declared, “Mark my words—I shall not apologize to you. You have had your victory this night, but I vow to seek your blood come morning!”

Jones dismissed the threat with a mocking laugh, while Mr. Maclachlan interjected, “Indeed, Mr. Fitzpatrick, you ought to feel shame for causing this uproar at such an ungodly hour. Remembering the connection between her quarters and Mr. Jones's, and trusting in his integrity, she cried out, “You are mistaken! I am wed to neither of you! Help! Rape! Murder! The landlady, now raising her voice to match the aggrieved woman's, lamented that her own reputation lay in tatters, shattered by the scene before them. The hour of night, and the behaviour of the man, who stared very wildly all the time, a little surprized Susan, so that she hesitated before she made any answer; upon which the gentleman, with redoubled eagerness, begged her to give him a true information, saying, He had lost his wife, and was come in pursuit of her.
