A tumultuous and fervent crowd surged, ebbing and flowing with fervid voices that rang out not as the dignified tones of a civilized gathering but as the raw howls of feral beasts driven by an insatiable thirst for retribution and scorn. As the sun slipped gracefully beneath the horizon, a sinister glow embraced the West Barricade—this infamy once adorned with the statue of a haughty tyrant, now merely a faint echo of his arrogance, a haunting symbol of a bygone national pride.

Throughout the day, the guillotine performed its grim duty with chilling accuracy, claiming the illustrious names steeped in France’s rich history—noble lineage and celebrated blood spilled as a sacrifice upon the altar of liberty and fraternity. Its horrific mechanism was momentarily halted as dusk enveloped the restless assembly, urging the increasingly agitated crowd toward more theatrical expressions, while the tattered remains of the barricades braced themselves against the encroaching shadows of night.

Unfettered, the throng surged from the Place de la Grève, irresistibly drawn to the barricades where mesmerizing spectacles lay in wait.

What had morphed into a grotesque performance now played out like an unsettling routine; oblivious aristocrats remained unaware of the ever-looming peril! Each individual—a traitor merely by their existence—embodied the descendants of noble clans that had basked in the affluence of France’s elite since the age of the Crusades. Their ancestors had ruthlessly oppressed the common folk, laying the burdens of their extravagant lifestyles upon the impoverished. Yet now, change swept through the land; the masses did not seek the annihilation of their oppressors, but rather swift justice delivered by the guillotine’s unrelenting blade.

Day after day, that dreadful instrument dispatched its ill-fated victims—the aged, the young women, the innocent—until the moment loomed near when not just any head would fall beneath its edge, but that of a King and his beguiling Queen.

This was the new reality: were the people not the legitimate rulers of France? Each aristocrat had become a traitor, mirroring their forebears; for two torturous centuries, the common folk endured suffering and starvation, all to maintain a court sunk in decadence. Now, the heirs of noble houses that once reveled in their dominance were in a desperate scramble, striving to evade the dreadful retribution that hung over them.

And flee they did, indulging in their own tragic farce. Each afternoon, just before the gates bolted shut and market carts rolled away, a hapless noble would attempt to slip past the ever-watchful Committee of Public Safety. They donned disguises, concocting countless ruses to navigate the heavily guarded barricades, where the citizen-soldiers of the Republic stood steadfast. Men masqueraded as women, women transformed into men, and ragged children evaded capture—all manner of desperate souls, from former counts to marquises and dukes—each one hoping to reach England or some distant haven, yearning to rally foreign allies against the daunting Revolution or to muster a force to liberate family members imprisoned in the Temple, the former stronghold of France's ruling elite.

Yet far too often, these unauthorized escapees fell prey to the sentinels at the gates. Sergeant Bibot, a formidable figure stationed at the West Gate, possessed an uncanny knack for unveiling even the most cunning disguises. Once a target was seized, the true spectacle began. Like a cat toying with a trapped mouse, he reveled in the moment, feigning ignorance of the wigs and fineries that concealed the real identities of noble marquises and counts.

Bibot was endowed with a wicked sense of humor, and lingering near the West Barricade was a rewarding pastime for him, simply to watch his masterful mockery of the fleeing aristocrats. 

At times, he would allow them a fleeting glimmer of hope, permitting a few tentative steps beyond the gate, only to summon men to drag them back, stripping away their disguises and revealing their true selves.

The scene was utterly absurd, particularly when a once-majestic marchioness found herself ensnared in Bibot’s trap, fully aware that a swift trial awaited her the next day, soon to be followed by the grim embrace of Madame la Guillotine.

On that unforgettable September afternoon, it was no surprise that the gathering at Bibot's gate simmered with anticipation. The collective thirst for blood intensified with each execution—an insatiable hunger that had witnessed the heads of a hundred noblemen roll beneath the blade, now eager for another hundred to meet the same fate at dawn.

Seated atop an overturned barrel near the gate, Bibot commanded a small contingent of citizens. His responsibilities had exploded; desperate aristocrats were in a frenzy, making desperate bids to flee Paris: men, women, and children whose ancestors had once served the loathed Bourbons, now branded as traitors awaiting the guillotine. Each day, Bibot relished the thrill of unmasking royalist fugitives, sending them back to face their fate before the Committee of Public Safety, under the watchful gaze of the esteemed patriot, Citoyen Foucquier-Tinville.

He had garnered praise from both Robespierre and Danton for his relentless pursuits, taking immense pride in claiming responsibility for the executions of no fewer than fifty aristocrats.

However, that day heralded a troubling change. Each sergeant stationed at the barricades received alarming orders. An unprecedented wave of aristocrats had managed to escape, finding refuge in England. Whispers of their daring flights spread like wildfire, igniting fear amongst the populace with every retelling. Sergeant Grospierre, facing severe consequences for allowing an entire family of aristocrats to slip through his grasp at the North Gate, became the target of public scorn.

Rumors circulated that these audacious escapes were orchestrated by a bold group of Englishmen meddling in affairs far beyond their concern, intent on rescuing those condemned to Madame la Guillotine. Strange stories proliferated, suggesting that the noble escapees vanished as they approached the barricades, slipping away as if cloaked in supernatural protection.

No one had laid eyes upon these figures, and whispers of their leader permeated the crowd, laced with ominous superstitions. As the day wore on, Citoyen Foucquier-Tinville frequently found himself handed folded letters—urgent warnings from strangers who stealthily slipped them into his pocket. Each note bore dire alerts about these meddlesome foreigners, signed with the insignia of a petite star-shaped flower known in England as the Scarlet Pimpernel. Mere hours after such brazen alerts reached the Committee, reports would arise of further royalists stealthily making their way to the coast, inching closer to safety in England.

The guards at the gates redoubled their vigilance; sergeants faced threats of execution; enticing rewards were promised for the capture of these daring Englishmen—five thousand francs for the elusive Scarlet Pimpernel.

A shared belief surged through the crowd; they were convinced that Bibot would be the one to capture him, and he, luxuriating in the anticipation, allowed the notion to simmer. Day after day, eager spectators flocked to the West Gate, anxious to witness Bibot ensnare any fleeing aristocrat alongside the legendary Englishman.

“Bah!” he scoffed to his trusted corporal. “Citoyen Grospierre was a fool! Had I manned that North Gate last week…”

Bibot spat onto the ground, his disdain for his colleague evident.

“What transpired, citoyen?” the corporal inquired, leaning closer.

"Grospierre was minding his post," Bibot recounted, swelling with pride as the crowd leaned in, eager to absorb his tale. "As you all know, this meddlesome Englishman, this wretched Scarlet Pimpernel, cannot pass through MY gate, MORBLEU! unless he has the devil himself as an ally. But Grospierre, that blundering buffoon, let a cart brimming with barrels roll through. It was driven by an old man and a boy, and Grospierre, feeling clever and slightly inebriated, peered inside the casks—most were empty—and let the cart continue on its way."

A wave of anger surged through the ragged assembly surrounding Citoyen Bibot.

"Half an hour later," he continued, "a guard captain burst in with a dozen soldiers. 'Did a cart pass through?' he barked. 'Yes,' Grospierre replied, 'not half an hour ago.' The captain, enraged, shouted, 'You let them escape! That cart concealed the CI-DEVANT Duc de Chalis and his entire family!' 'What!' Grospierre exclaimed, his eyes wide with disbelief. 'Indeed, and the driver was that loathsome Englishman, the Scarlet Pimpernel.'"

A chorus of condemnation surged through the crowd. Citoyen Grospierre had paid with his life for that grievous error, and what a monumental folly it had been!

Bibot chuckled at the absurdity, struggling to compose himself before continuing.

"'After them, my men!' the captain commanded. 'Remember the reward! Pursue them! They cannot have gone far!' And with that, he dashed through the gate, leading his squad."

"But it was far too late!" the crowd clamored, relishing the bittersweet irony.

“They missed their chance!”

“Cursed Grospierre for his folly!”

“He deserved his fate!”

“How could he have overlooked those barrels?”

Yet these grievances only seemed to amuse Citoyen Bibot further; he laughed until tears streamed down his cheeks.

A hush fell over the gathering; the tale took on an otherworldly quality, and although the Republic claimed to have renounced God, it had not extinguished the deep-seated fears of the mystical that lingered in the hearts of the people. Truly, that Englishman must be the devil himself.

As the sun dipped lower in the sky, Bibot braced himself for the gates' closure.

With one final raucous laugh, both dismissive and defiant, the old woman cracked her whip and urged her bony nag through the gate.

That encounter left a pall over the afternoon. The people trembled at the thought of such malignant curses—two diseases that could herald unspeakable suffering. Ewin Mackinnon is dead, I know; for five years ago come Martinmas night I saw his perjured soul on its way to hell. All the world is turning Whig. A man may hate the world, it is true, but he needs a single foe."


"And in that capacity you have adopted me?" demanded Haward.


MacLean let his gaze travel over the man opposite him, from the looped hat and the face between the waves of hair to the gilt spurs upon the great boots; then turned his eyes upon his own hand and coarsely clad arm stretched across the cask. "I, too, am a gentleman, the brother of a chieftain," he declared. "I am not without schooling. I have seen something of life, and of countries more polite than the land where I was born, though not so dear. I have been free, and have loved my freedom. Do you find it so strange that I should hate you?"


There was a silence; then, "Upon my soul, I do not know that I do," said Haward slowly. "And yet, until this day I did not know of your existence."


"But I knew of yours," answered the storekeeper. "Your agent hath an annoying trick of speech, and the overseers have caught it from him. 'Your master' this, and 'your master' that; in short, for ten years it hath been, 'Work, you dog, that your master may play!' Well, I have worked; it was that, or killing myself, or going mad. I have worked for you in the fields, in the smithy, in this close room. But when you bought my body, you could not buy my soul. Day after day, and night after night, I sent it away; I would not let it bide in these dull levels, in this cursed land of heat and stagnant waters. At first it went home to its own country,--to its friends and its foes, to the torrent and the mountain and the music of the pipes; but at last the pain outweighed the pleasure, and I sent it there no more. And then it began to follow you."


"To follow me!" involuntarily exclaimed Haward.


"I have been in London," went on the other, without heeding the interruption. "I know the life of men of quality, and where they most resort. I early learned from your other servants, and from the chance words of those who had your affairs in charge, that you were young, well-looking, a man of pleasure. At first when I thought of you the blood came into my cheek, but at last I thought of you constantly, and I felt for you a constant hatred. It began when I knew that Ewin Mackinnon was dead. I had no need of love; I had need of hate. Day after day, my body slaving here, my mind has dogged your footsteps. Up and down, to and fro, in business and in pleasure, in whatever place I have imagined you to be, there have I been also. Did you never, when there seemed none by, look over your shoulder, feeling another presence than your own?"


He ceased to speak, and the hand upon the cask was still. The sunshine was clean gone from the room, and without the door the wind in the locust-tree answered the voice of the river. Haward rose from his seat, but made no further motion toward departing. "You have been frank," he said quietly. "Had you it in mind, all this while, so to speak to me when we should meet?"


"No," answered the other. "I thought not of words, but of"--


"But of deeds," Haward finished for him. "Rather, I imagine, of one deed."


Composed as ever in voice and manner, he drew out his watch, and held it aslant that the light might strike upon the dial. "'T is after six," he remarked as he put it away, "and I am yet a mile from the house." The wine that he had poured for himself had been standing, untouched, upon the keg beside him. He took it up and drank it off; then wiped his lips with his handkerchief, and passing the storekeeper with a slight inclination of his head walked toward the door. A yard beyond the man who had so coolly shown his side of the shield was a rude table, on which were displayed hatchets and hunting knives. Haward passed the gleaming steel; then, a foot beyond it, stood still, his face to the open door, and his back to the storekeeper and the table with its sinister lading.


"You do wrong to allow so much dust and disorder," he said sharply. "I could write my name in that mirror, and there is a piece of brocade fallen to the floor. Look to it that you keep the place more neat."


There was dead silence for a moment; then MacLean spoke in an even voice: "Now a fool might call you as brave as Hector. For myself, I only give you credit for some knowledge of men. You are right. It is not my way to strike in the back an unarmed man. When you are gone, I will wipe off the mirror and pick up the brocade."


He followed Haward outside. "It's a brave evening for riding," he remarked, "and you have a bonny bit of horseflesh there. You'll get to the house before candlelight."


Beside one of the benches Haward made another pause. "You are a Highlander and a Jacobite," he said. "From your reference to Forster, I gather that you were among the prisoners taken at Preston and transported to Virginia."


"In the Elizabeth and Anne of Liverpool, _alias_ a bit of hell afloat; the master, Captain Edward Trafford, _alias_ Satan's first mate," quoth the other grimly.


He stooped to the bench where lay the débris of the coast and mountains he had been lately building, and picked up a small, deep shell. "My story is short," he began. "It could be packed into this. I was born in the island of Mull, of my father a chieftain, and my mother a lady. Some schooling I got in Aberdeen, some pleasure in Edinburgh and London, and some service abroad. In my twenty-third year--being at home at that time--I was asked to a hunting match at Braemar, and went. No great while afterwards I was bidden to supper at an Edinburgh tavern, and again I accepted the invitation. There was a small entertainment to follow the supper,--just the taking of Edinburgh Castle. But the wine was good, and we waited to powder our hair, and the entertainment could hardly be called a success. Hard upon that convivial evening, I, with many others, was asked across the Border to join a number of gentlemen who drank to the King after our fashion, and had a like fancy for oak boughs and white roses. The weather was pleasant, the company of the best, the roads very noble after our Highland sheep tracks. Together with our English friends, and enlivened by much good claret and by music of bagpipe and drum, we strolled on through a fine, populous country until we came to a town called Preston, where we thought we would tarry for a day or two. However, circumstances arose which detained us somewhat longer. (I dare say you have heard the story?) When finally we took our leave, some of us went to heaven, some to hell, and some to Barbadoes and Virginia. I was among those dispatched to Virginia, and to all intents and purposes I died the day I landed. There, the shell is full!"


He tossed it from him, and going to the hitching-post loosed Haward's horse. Haward took the reins from his hand. "It hath been ten years and more since Virginia got her share of the rebels taken at Preston. If I remember aright, their indentures were to be made for seven years. Why, then, are you yet in my service?"


MacLean laughed. "I ran away," he replied pleasantly, "and when I was caught I made off a second time. I wonder that you planters do not have a Society for the Encouragement of Runaways. Seeing that they are nearly always retaken, and that their escapades so lengthen their term of service, it would surely be to your advantage! There are yet several years in which I am to call you master."


He laughed again, but the sound was mirthless, and the eyes beneath the half-closed lids were harder than steel. Haward mounted his horse and gathered up the reins. "I am not responsible for the laws of the realm," he said calmly, "nor for rebellions and insurrections, nor for the practice of transporting overseas those to whom have been given the ugly names of 'rebel' and 'traitor.' Destiny that set you there put me here. We are alike pawns; what the player means we have no way of telling. Curse Fate and the gods, if you choose,--and find that your cursing does small good,--but regard me with indifference, as one neither more nor less the slave of circumstances than yourself. It has been long since I went this way. Is there yet the path by the river?"


"Ay," answered the other. "It is your shortest road."


"Then I will be going," said Haward. "It grows late, and I am not looked for before to-morrow. Good-night."


As he spoke he raised his hat and bowed to the gentleman from whom he was parting. That rebel to King George gave a great start; then turned very red, and shot a piercing glance at the man on horseback. The latter's mien was composed as ever, and, with his hat held beneath his arm and his body slightly inclined, he was evidently awaiting a like ceremony of leave-taking on the storekeeper's part. MacLean drew a long breath, stepped back a pace or two, and bowed to his equal. A second "Good-night," and one gentleman rode off in the direction of the great house, while the other went thoughtfully back to the store, got a cloth and wiped the dust from the mirror.

Make this passage sound less AI and more human:
In the softly lit debate room designated for the visiting committee, Miss White once again demonstrated her considerable influence. As the vice president of the board of managers, she felt it was her solemn duty to investigate and address any issues requiring urgent attention.

"Mrs. Mason, could you please clarify who arranged for the delivery of that book to us?" she asked, her gaze steady and determined.

"Eugene Rutland, who was previously in Mrs. Williams' care, is behind it. He has since been adopted by Mr. Graham and is now known as Eugene Graham. Though they aren’t biologically related, he harbors a deep affection for Beulah," Mrs. Mason explained.

"He left the asylum long before I joined the board. What sort of person is he? I’ve met him a couple of times and found him rather unremarkable."

"Oh, my dear! He is anything but forgettable! Leaving him behind three years ago broke my heart. He is significantly older than Beulah and cares for her with the love and devotion of an older brother," Mrs. Williams passionately defended her choice to her fellow board member.

"I trust he encourages her ambition of becoming a teacher, though that dream must be set aside. There’s an opportunity for her—she could earn six dollars a month as a babysitter. We must secure it for her."

"Oh, Miss White! Beulah simply doesn’t have the strength to consistently care for a larger child!" Mrs. Williams protested.

"She is entirely capable! Trust me, this experience will be invaluable for her before the month is out." Just then, Beulah appeared in the hallway, a whisper of encouragement fluttering through her mind, declaring, "You are destined for greatness." Instinctively, she covered her ears, seeking refuge from Miss Dorothea's sharp voice and retreated, her heart gripped by an unsettling wave of dread.

The next day dawned with a sense of gratitude, ushered in by the mayor, as the residents of the asylum were guided to the morning service at the church. After a modest midday meal, the matron granted an unusual afternoon of freedom, permitting the children to explore. An exhilarating wave of joy swept through the group, each child scattering in different directions as Beulah chose to stay close to Mrs. Williams.

"Mrs. Williams, may I take Lilly to explore the woods behind the asylum?" she asked, her eyes shimmering with excitement.

"I’m afraid you must stay here this evening, though it truly pains me to say so," the matron replied, her voice heavy with regret.

"Oh, that’s perfectly alright! I’m more than willing to assist with anything you need," Beulah responded cheerfully.

Tears welled in the matron's eyes, prompting her to quickly avert her gaze, hastily wiping them away with her apron.

"Is something wrong? How can I help?" Beulah asked, concern furrowing her brow.

"Never mind, dear Beulah. Just take your bonnet and stay near the edge of the woods—not too far; if I need you, I’ll send someone for you."

"If my presence is a burden, I would rather stay here."

"Oh, my dear, you are no burden at all. I genuinely wish for you to enjoy yourself." With that, the matron turned away, leaving Beulah enveloped in a longing to follow her and learn more about her future. Yet, an unsettling anxiety settled deep in her chest. "It will reveal itself in time," she whispered softly to herself as she took a step forward.

"May I join you and Lilly?" piped up little Claudia, darting along the path and peering through the fence.

"Of course! You and Lilly can collect smooth burrs for basket-making. But where's your bonnet?" Beulah teased.

"I forgot it!" Claudia exclaimed, nearly breathless as she grabbed Beulah's hand.

"You’ve let it slip your mind again! You little rascal, you’ll turn as dark as a gypsy!" Beulah chuckled.

"I don’t mind! I absolutely can’t stand bonnets," Claudia replied defiantly.

"Be cautious, Claudy; you know Miss White doesn’t want you returning freckled and sunburned."

"Will she really care?" Claudia shot back, mischief sparkling in her dark eyes.

"Oh, she certainly will. Now, wear my hood. And if you chase after me again without a hat, I’ll send you back for one; clear?"

"Yes, I understand. I wonder why Miss Dorothy doesn’t try to lighten her freckles; she looks like a—"

"Hush! Let's not talk about her for now. Just run ahead."

"Can we pause for a moment? I need to catch my breath. Where are we headed?"

"To the pine woods," Lilly exclaimed, clapping her hands in delight. "We’re going to have so much fun rolling and sliding on the straw!" The two girls dashed away, their carefree steps echoing toward a hollow where the earth gently rose into hills thickly cloaked in pines. Beulah settled atop a mound of moss and leaves while Claudia and Lilly eagerly discarded their hoods, diving into their sliding game. The pine needles created a slick path, allowing them to glide down the slope, tumbling and rolling in sheer bliss. Their laughter rang through the trees, harmonizing with the cheerful melodies of the birds flitting nearby.

Yet, Beulah felt like a distant observer of their delight. Contemplating the weighty words of the matron, she lingered at the edge of the woods, ensuring she could still catch glimpses of the asylum's white fence. The winter wind whispered through the pine needles, weaving a bittersweet melody of nature that she often missed. With every breath infused with the scent of rustling branches, she stretched her arms toward the sky, longing to embrace the splendid symphony of life. Above her, the azure sky loomed like a vigilant guardian, while sunlight danced among the brown leaves and gnarled trunks, sometimes caressing them gently, sometimes retreating behind fleeting shadows.

For a brief moment, Beulah surrendered to the tranquil beauty that enveloped her. Her appreciation for nature ran deep, fueled by the infrequency of joyful moments in her existence, causing her spirit to soar in harmony with the birds, trees, flowers, sunshine, and stars—all melding with the whispers of the wind. A beloved copy of Longfellow's poems rested in her lap, its pages marked at “Excelsior” and “The Psalm of Life.” The stirrings within her heart mirrored the ebb and flow of emotions elicited by her communion with nature. A radiant glimmer brightened her typically troubled gray eyes, filling them with unwavering hope. As a sacred hymn floated through the evening air, she began to sing from the pages of her cherished book:

    "Tell me not in mournful numbers,
     Life is but an empty dream;
     For the soul is dead that slumbers,
     And things are not what they seem."

The richness and sweetness of her voice were captivating, each note cascading from her lips with delicate resonance. Her heart resonated profoundly with the poet's sentiments, urging her to ardently recite the subsequent lines:

    "In the world’s broad field of battle,
     In the bivouac of life;
     Be not like dumb, driven cattle,
     Be a hero in the strife."

A disquieting flutter stirred within her, igniting a realization of the challenges that lay ahead, compelling her to brace for the storms to come. With a heart brimming with hope and steadfast determination, she steeled herself for whatever awaited. Yet, as the final note lingered in the air, she lowered her head onto her arms, shadows of anxiety casting their pall over her features. Only the Great Shepherd understood the silent laments that lingered on her pale lips.

Suddenly, a sharp bark from a nearby dog jolted her from her reverie. She looked up to see a gentleman leaning against a nearby tree, watching her intently. As their eyes met, he approached with a warm smile. "Rest assured, my dog means you no harm. Like his master, he wouldn’t dream of disturbing you until you’ve finished your song. Down, Carlo; quiet now. May I ask who taught you to sing?"

Beulah sprang to her feet, her cheeks tinged with warmth at the question. Though inherently shy, she radiated an unusual confidence for someone of her age. "I’ve never had a teacher, sir; I simply listen to the choir during services and sing our Sunday school hymns at church," she replied softly.

"Do you know who penned the words you just sang? I had no idea they were set to music."

"I came across them in this book yesterday and loved them so much that I attempted to set them to one of our hymn tunes," she explained, lifting the volume for him to peruse.

He glanced at the title, curiosity illuminating his expression. At that moment, Beulah noticed one of the older girls from the asylum darting across the lawn, a wave of worry flooding her mind as she sought Claudia and Lilly, who had temporarily abandoned their sliding to gather pine burrs.

"Come along, Claudy and Lilly! The matron has sent for us; we must hurry!" she called out.

"Do you live at the asylum?" the gentleman inquired, brushing ash from his cigar.

"Yes, sir," she replied. Just as her companions arrived, she offered a courteous nod before turning to walk back.

"Wait a moment. Surely these aren’t your sisters?" he remarked, admiration glinting in his gaze as he took in their beauty.

"This one is mine, sir," she gestured toward Lillian, "but the other is not." Claudia shyly glanced at the stranger, tightening her grip on Beulah’s dress. "Oh, Beulah, please don’t let us go just yet! I’ve left a massive pile of burrs behind!"

"We truly must return; look, here comes Katy to fetch us. Good evening, sir."

"Good evening, my little friends. I shall make it a point to visit the asylum soon, and I hope to hear that lovely song again."

Beulah remained silent, gripping her sister’s hand tightly as they hurried home. Katy relayed Mrs. Williams' message, emphasizing the urgency as Miss Dorothy had grown upset about the children's prolonged absence.

"What? Is she here again, that dreadful—" Beulah swiftly silenced Claudia’s words with a hand over her mouth. The brief return felt fraught with the tension of clashing emotions swirling within Beulah's heart, her hold on Lillian’s hand tightening.

"Oh, what a beautiful carriage!" Claudia exclaimed, captivated by a magnificent vehicle adorned with silver accents, drawn by two spirited black horses.

"Indeed, the lady and gentleman inside must be quite wealthy, judging by their appearance. Miss White is accompanying them," Beulah noted.

"What do they want, Katy?" Claudia asked, her eyes wide with curiosity.

"I can’t say for certain, but I have my suspicions," Katy replied, a knowing smile flickering across her face, further fraying Beulah’s nerves.

"Come along, Beulah, take them up to the dormitory," Mrs. Williams instructed upon meeting them at the entrance, ushering them upstairs. In a whirlwind of activity, she washed Claudia’s face and re-curled her hair, meticulously tending to Lillian as well.

"Don’t scrub my hand so harshly; you’re hurting me!" Claudia protested, wincing beneath the matron's careful ministrations.

"I only want you clean and beautiful, my dear," Mrs. Williams replied gently.

"Well, I assure you, it won’t wash off—it’s turpentine," Claudia retorted defiantly.

"Come now, Beulah; bring Lilly with you. Miss White is growing impatient," Mrs. Williams urged.

"What is all this about?" Beulah asked, a frown of confusion knitting her brows as she grasped her sister's hand.

"Do not dwell on it, dear child." With a compassionate glance, the matron guided them into the reception room, where none of the other children were present. Beulah immediately sensed an unsettling tension in the air; the atmosphere felt charged. Miss White animatedly conversed with an elegantly dressed woman, while a gentleman nervously fiddled with his seal and watch key. The focus shifted as Miss White exclaimed, "Here they are! My dear Mrs. Grayson, I believe you will find what you seek. Come here, little ones."

Drawing Claudia close, she beckoned the children while Lillian remained steadfastly by Beulah's side.

"Oh, how lovely they are! Just look at them, Alfred!" Mrs. Grayson exclaimed, her eyes sparkling with delight as they flitted from girl to girl.

"Indeed, very pretty, my dear. Handsome children, particularly the one with the dark eyes," her husband remarked, his tone markedly less enthusiastic.

"I have a fondness for the fair-haired one; she resembles a perfect little fairy. Come here, my dear, let me speak with you," she continued, reaching out for Lillian. The little girl tightened her grip on Beulah’s fingers, unwilling to budge.

"Do not hold her back, Beulah. Lillian, come to the lady," Miss White insisted. Reluctantly loosening her hold, Beulah felt her very hope slipping away. Prompted by her sister's words, Lillian hesitantly took a step forward, pausing just before the stranger. Mrs. Grayson gently clasped the child’s delicate hands and planted a soft kiss on her lips. "What is your name, sweetheart?" she asked kindly.

"Lillian, ma'am; but my sister calls me Lilly."

"Who is ‘sister’—this little one?" she pointed at Claudia.

"Oh, no; that’s Sister Beulah." The affection reflected in Lillian’s soft blue eyes highlighted the profound bond she shared with her sister.

"My goodness, Alfred; how completely different they are! This child is among the most beautiful I’ve ever encountered, while that girl over there is not," Mrs. Grayson whispered to her husband, who was deep in conversation with Claudia. Though her words were barely audible, Beulah caught every inflection, a rush of heat flooding her cheeks with shame. Claudia, too, caught the remark, springing from Mr. Grayson’s lap in defiance. "She isn’t ugly at all! She’s the smartest girl in the asylum, and I love her more than anyone!"

"While Beulah may not align with conventional beauty standards, her goodness speaks volumes," Mrs. Williams interjected, placing a comforting hand on Beulah's shoulder. A flicker of bitterness crossed Beulah's lips, yet her gaze remained fixated on Lillian's face.

"Fanny, if you choose that outspoken one, you’ll have your hands full," Mr. Grayson commented, amusement sparkling in his eyes.

"Oh, Alfred, I simply must adopt both of them. Imagine how enchanting they will look, dressed in matching outfits! My dear Lilly and you too, Claudia—will you come and be my daughters? I will love you dearly, and that gentleman will be your father. He is very kind. You will have tall dolls with beautiful dresses, dollhouses, tea sets, and every evening, I shall take you for rides in my carriage. As Beulah listened, the blood drained from her face. The harsh reality of potential separation pierced her for the first time, and staggering forward, she clutched the matron's dress, crying out, "Oh, please don’t take Lilly away! I would do anything—anything! Please, don’t take my darling Lilly!"

Claudia, sensing the gravity of the moment, added urgently, "I would gladly go, but only if Beulah comes too. Lilly, are you going?"

"No, no!" Lilly cried, wrenching herself from the stranger's grasp and sprinting back to her sister; however, Miss White quickly extended her arms, holding her back with tender strength. In a panic, Lilly burst into tears, pleading, "Oh, sister! Take me with you!"

Beulah rushed to her side, her voice fierce and unwavering, "Give her to me! She belongs to me, and you have no right to separate us!" She reached out toward the struggling child.

"Lilly, my precious darling!" Beulah leaned closer, but just as Mrs. Williams lifted the child from the ground, Lilly wrapped her little arms tightly around Beulah's neck.

"Leave your worries behind, Alfred. In merely a few days, we will manage splendidly. How proud I will be to showcase such precious gems!"

In the debating room of the visiting committee Miss White again had the floor. She was no less important a personage than vice president of the board of managers, and felt authorized to investigate closely and redress all grievances.


"Who did you say sent that book here, Mrs. Mason?"

After an early dinner, the matron gave them permission to amuse themselves the remainder of the day as their various inclinations prompted. There was an immediate dispersion of the assemblage, and only Beulah lingered beside the matron's chair.


"Mrs. Williams, may I take Lilly with me, and go out into the woods at the back of the asylum?"


"I want you at home this evening; but I dislike very much to refuse you."


"Oh, never mind! if you wish me to do anything," answered the girl cheerfully.

"Can I do anything to help you? What is the matter?"


"Never mind, Beulah; do you get your bonnet and go to the edge of the woods--not too far, remember; and if I must have you, why I will send for you."


"I would rather not go if it will be any trouble."

"You forgot it, indeed! You little witch, you will burn as black as a gypsy!"


"I don't care if I do. I hate bonnets."


"Take care, Claudy; the President won't have you all freckled and tanned."


"Won't he?" queried the child, with a saucy sparkle in her black eyes.


"That he won't. Here, tie on my hood, and the next time you come running after me bareheaded, I will make you go back; do you hear?"


"Yes, I hear. I wonder why Miss Dorothy don't bleach off her freckles; she looks like a--"


"Hush about her, and run on ahead."


"Do, pray, let me get my breath first. Which way are we going?"


"To the piney woods yonder," cried Lilly, clapping her hands in childish glee; "won't we have fun, rolling and sliding on the straw?" The two little ones walked on in advance. At last, St. John broke the quiet, “Damn! Damn everything! Damn everyone!” he added fervently. “At Cambridge, there are people worth engaging with.”

“Indeed, Cambridge does boast some intriguing characters,” Helen replied, her tone calm and detached. Then, snapping back to the moment, she inquired, “By the way, have you made any decisions regarding your future—Cambridge or the Bar?”

He pressed his lips together tightly, pausing to collect his thoughts while Helen remained absorbed, observing Rachel and pondering which of the two young men might capture her interest. Spotting Hirst, she mused, “He’s rather unattractive. It’s a pity they’re all so plain.”

She exempted Hewet from this judgment; her mind wandered to the intelligent, honest, and engaging young men she knew—Hirst included—wondering why sharp intellect and scholarly pursuits often overshadowed physical allure, with mental acumen soaring to dazzling heights while everything else faded into obscurity.

“And what of the future?” she reflected, contemplating a reality in which men increasingly resembled Hirst and women mirrored Rachel. “Oh no,” she concluded, casting another glance at him, “marrying you would be far from ideal. The future of humanity might hinge on Susan and Arthur; no—that thought is profoundly unsettling. Perhaps it’s the laborers; surely not the English, but rather the Russians and Chinese.” These troubling reflections filled her with dissatisfaction, abruptly interrupted as St. John pressed on:

“I wish you could meet Bennett. He’s the most remarkable man alive.”

“Bennett?” she asked, intrigued. In that moment, St. John relaxed, shedding his earlier intensity as he detailed Bennett, who dwelled in an ancient windmill six miles from Cambridge. He led what St. John described as a wholesome life—solitary and simple, entirely devoted to truth, ever open to discussion yet astonishingly humble in his brilliance.

“Don’t you think,” he continued after extolling Bennett, “that such authenticity makes the rest of us appear rather trivial? Did you notice Hewet’s struggle during the tea conversation? It felt like everyone else was poised to pounce on me, eager for some scandalous utterance. But it was nothing of the sort. If Bennett had been there, he would have stated his thoughts clearly or simply walked away. There’s a bitterness in such dynamics—unless one possesses Bennett’s strength of character. It can be rather disheartening. Do you perceive me as bitter?”

Helen opted for silence, urging him to continue:

“Indeed, I am deeply bitter, and it is a wretched state to endure. But perhaps my gravest flaw is envy. I envy everyone. The idea of others surpassing me—even in trivial matters—gnaws at me—like waiters adroitly balancing towering piles of plates—even Arthur, simply because Susan dotes on him. I crave the approval of others; it forever eludes me. Of course, it likely stems, in part, from my appearance,” he mused, “although it would be disingenuous to claim any Jewish heritage—my family has resided in Norfolk for at least three centuries, much like Hirst of Hirstbourne Hall. It must be profoundly soothing to possess what you have—everyone adoring you.”

“I assure you, that’s not the case,” Helen responded with a light-hearted laugh.

“Indeed, it is,” Hirst maintained with unwavering conviction. “Firstly, you are the most beautiful woman I’ve ever encountered; secondly, you possess an extraordinarily kind spirit.”

Had Hirst dared to meet Helen’s gaze, he might have noticed the warmth flooding her cheeks—partly from delight, partly from a growing affection for the young man who, despite his unremarkable exterior and seemingly understated demeanor, had unexpectedly stirred her empathy. She sensed his unvoiced turmoil and felt drawn to him, for many of his reflections resonated deeply; she admired the moral integrity of youth yet felt an irresistible urge to escape into something vibrant and impersonal she could grasp. Retreating into the house, she returned with her embroidery. Yet he remained oblivious to her presence, his gaze still lost in distant reverie.

“About Miss Vinrace,” he began, “oh, let’s not delve into the realm of St. John and Helen, and Rachel and Terence—what is she like? Is she rational, does she feel deeply, or is she merely a stagnant footstool?”

"But about Gibbon?" Hewet interrupted. The look of nervous tension which had come over every face was relaxed by the interruption.
"You find him monotonous, I suppose. But you know--" He opened the book, and began searching for passages to read aloud, and in a little time he found a good one which he considered suitable. But there was nothing in the world that bored Ridley more than being read aloud to, and he was besides scrupulously fastidious as to the dress and behaviour of ladies. In the space of fifteen minutes he had decided against Mrs. Flushing on the ground that her orange plume did not suit her complexion, that she spoke too loud, that she crossed her legs, and finally, when he saw her accept a cigarette that Hewet offered her, he jumped up, exclaiming something about "bar parlours," and left them. Mrs. Flushing was evidently relieved by his departure. She puffed her cigarette, stuck her legs out, and examined Helen closely as to the character and reputation of their common friend Mrs. Raymond Parry. By a series of little strategems she drove her to define Mrs. Parry as somewhat elderly, by no means beautiful, very much made up--an insolent old harridan, in short, whose parties were amusing because one met odd people; but Helen herself always pitied poor Mr. Parry, who was understood to be shut up downstairs with cases full of gems, while his wife enjoyed herself in the drawing-room. "Not that I believe what people say against her--although she hints, of course--" Upon which Mrs. Flushing cried out with delight:

"She's my first cousin! Go on--go on!"

When Mrs. Flushing rose to go she was obviously delighted with her new acquaintances. She made three or four different plans for meeting or going on an expedition, or showing Helen the things they had bought, on her way to the carriage. She included them all in a vague but magnificent invitation.

As Helen returned to the garden again, Ridley's words of warning came into her head, and she hesitated a moment and looked at Rachel sitting between Hirst and Hewet. But she could draw no conclusions, for Hewet was still reading Gibbon aloud, and Rachel, for all the expression she had, might have been a shell, and his words water rubbing against her ears, as water rubs a shell on the edge of a rock.

Hewet's voice was very pleasant. When he reached the end of the period Hewet stopped, and no one volunteered any criticism.

"I do adore the aristocracy!" Hirst exclaimed after a moment's pause. "They're so amazingly unscrupulous. None of us would dare to behave as that woman behaves."

"What I like about them," said Helen as she sat down, "is that they're so well put together. Naked, Mrs. Flushing would be superb. Dressed as she dresses, it's absurd, of course."

"Yes," said Hirst. A shade of depression crossed his face. "I've never weighed more than ten stone in my life," he said, "which is ridiculous, considering my height, and I've actually gone down in weight since we came here. I daresay that accounts for the rheumatism." Again he jerked his wrist back sharply, so that Helen might hear the grinding of the chalk stones. She could not help smiling.

"It's no laughing matter for me, I assure you," he protested. "My mother's a chronic invalid, and I'm always expecting to be told that I've got heart disease myself. Rheumatism always goes to the heart in the end."

"For goodness' sake, Hirst," Hewet protested; "one might think you were an old cripple of eighty. If it comes to that, I had an aunt who died of cancer myself, but I put a bold face on it--" He rose and began tilting his chair backwards and forwards on its hind legs. "Is any one here inclined for a walk?" he said. "There's a magnificent walk, up behind the house. You come out on to a cliff and look right down into the sea. The rocks are all red; you can see them through the water. The other day I saw a sight that fairly took my breath away--about twenty jelly-fish, semi-transparent, pink, with long streamers, floating on the top of the waves."

"Sure they weren't mermaids?" said Hirst. "It's much too hot to climb uphill." He looked at Helen, who showed no signs of moving.

"Yes, it's too hot," Helen decided.

There was a short silence.

"I'd like to come," said Rachel.

"But she might have said that anyhow," Helen thought to herself as Hewet and Rachel went away together, and Helen was left alone with St. John, to St. John's obvious satisfaction.


He may have been satisfied, but his usual difficulty in deciding that one subject was more deserving of notice than another prevented him from speaking for some time. He sat staring intently at the head of a dead match, while Helen considered--so it seemed from the expression of her eyes--something not closely connected with the present moment.

At last St. John exclaimed, "Damn! Damn everything! Damn everybody!" he added. "At Cambridge there are people to talk to."

"At Cambridge there are people to talk to," Helen echoed him, rhythmically and absent-mindedly. Then she woke up. "By the way, have you settled what you're going to do--is it to be Cambridge or the Bar?"

He pursed his lips, but made no immediate answer, for Helen was still slightly inattentive. She had been thinking about Rachel and which of the two young men she was likely to fall in love with, and now sitting opposite to Hirst she thought, "He's ugly. It's a pity they're so ugly."

She did not include Hewet in this criticism; she was thinking of the clever, honest, interesting young men she knew, of whom Hirst was a good example, and wondering whether it was necessary that thought and scholarship should thus maltreat their bodies, and should thus elevate their minds to a very high tower from which the human race appeared to them like rats and mice squirming on the flat.

"And the future?" she reflected, vaguely envisaging a race of men becoming more and more like Hirst, and a race of women becoming more and more like Rachel. "Oh no," she concluded, glancing at him, "one wouldn't marry you. Well, then, the future of the race is in the hands of Susan and Arthur; no--that's dreadful. Of farm labourers; no--not of the English at all, but of Russians and Chinese." This train of thought did not satisfy her, and was interrupted by St. John, who began again:

"I wish you knew Bennett. He's the greatest man in the world."

"Bennett?" she enquired. Becoming more at ease, St. John dropped the concentrated abruptness of his manner, and explained that Bennett was a man who lived in an old windmill six miles out of Cambridge. He lived the perfect life, according to St. John, very lonely, very simple, caring only for the truth of things, always ready to talk, and extraordinarily modest, though his mind was of the greatest.

"Don't you think," said St. John, when he had done describing him, "that kind of thing makes this kind of thing rather flimsy? Did you notice at tea how poor old Hewet had to change the conversation? How they were all ready to pounce upon me because they thought I was going to say something improper? It wasn't anything, really. If Bennett had been there he'd have said exactly what he meant to say, or he'd have got up and gone. But there's something rather bad for the character in that--I mean if one hasn't got Bennett's character. It's inclined to make one bitter. Should you say that I was bitter?"

Helen did not answer, and he continued:

"Of course I am, disgustingly bitter, and it's a beastly thing to be. But the worst of me is that I'm so envious. I envy every one. I can't endure people who do things better than I do--perfectly absurd things too--waiters balancing piles of plates--even Arthur, because Susan's in love with him. I want people to like me, and they don't. It's partly my appearance, I expect," he continued, "though it's an absolute lie to say I've Jewish blood in me--as a matter of fact we've been in Norfolk, Hirst of Hirstbourne Hall, for three centuries at least. It must be awfully soothing to be like you--every one liking one at once."

"I assure you they don't," Helen laughed.

"They do," said Hirst with conviction. "In the first place, you're the most beautiful woman I've ever seen; in the second, you have an exceptionally nice nature."

If Hirst had looked at her instead of looking intently at his teacup he would have seen Helen blush, partly with pleasure, partly with an impulse of affection towards the young man who had seemed, and would seem again, so ugly and so limited. She pitied him, for she suspected that he suffered, and she was interested in him, for many of the things he said seemed to her true; she admired the morality of youth, and yet she felt imprisoned. As if her instinct were to escape to something brightly coloured and impersonal, which she could hold in her hands, she went into the house and returned with her embroidery. But he was not interested in her embroidery; he did not even look at it.

"About Miss Vinrace," he began,--"oh, look here, do let's be St. John and Helen, and Rachel and Terence--what's she like? Does she reason, does she feel, or is she merely a kind of footstool?"
